meta.regex_dialect: Python re. Patterns were authored for JavaScript and converted; the review page may need \Z replaced with $ (no multiline).

scope_semantics.sentence: a match anywhere counts (min_matches applies per text)
scope_semantics.text: count matches across the whole text

scan_semantics.prose: code blocks, inline code, URLs, and blockquotes are masked before matching

rules.name: Write to one specific reader
rules.dont: Text aimed at nobody in particular: "users", "stakeholders", "the reader", "one", and explanations pitched at the writer's own level of knowledge.
rules.do: Picture one real person who will read it, what they already know, and what they need to do next. Write to them as "you".
rules.rationale: Pinker calls the curse of knowledge the chief cause of opaque writing: writers can't remember what it was like not to know. Buffett's fix, in the SEC handbook's preface, is to write for one smart non-expert he knows.
detect: Third-person references to the reader ('the user', 'users', 'one') in text the reader will act on
Undefined steps the writer skipped because they're obvious to the writer
rules.exceptions: Specs and reports about users (not to them) can use 'users'.

examples.bad: Users should ensure that the configuration file is updated prior to deployment.
examples.better: Before you deploy, update config.toml.

examples.bad: One may wish to consult the documentation for further details.
examples.better: The setup steps are in README.md.

examples.bad: Stakeholders will need to review the proposal.
examples.better: Maria and the finance team need to approve this by Friday.

rules.source: SEC Plain English Handbook (1998) (Buffett preface); Pinker, The Sense of Style (2014); Federal Plain Language Guidelines (plainlanguage.gov / digital.gov); Google developer documentation style guide; 18F content guide

rules.name: Start with the familiar, end with the new
rules.dont: Sentences that open with new, unexplained information and end on old or minor detail, and subjects separated from their verbs by long interruptions.
rules.do: Open each sentence with something the reader already knows (often from the previous sentence). Put the subject's verb right after it. Save the new or important part for the end, where readers put emphasis.
rules.rationale: Gopen and Swan showed readers expect context at the start of a sentence (topic position) and emphasis at the end (stress position). Williams calls this old-to-new cohesion.
detect: A long phrase (8+ words) between the subject and its verb
A sentence whose first words are new to the reader while its last words repeat known material
Paragraphs where each sentence starts on a different topic
rules.exceptions: Gopen and Swan call these reader expectations, not rules. Break them on purpose for effect.

examples.bad: The enzyme, purified from bacterial cultures grown for three days under a modified protocol, increased the reaction rate.
examples.better: We grew bacterial cultures for three days under an adjusted protocol and purified the enzyme. Adding it increased the reaction rate.
examples.note: Adapted from Gopen and Swan's subject-verb principle.

examples.bad: A new retry policy, which the platform team designed after last month's outage, is now the default.
examples.better: Last month's outage led the platform team to design a new retry policy. That policy is now the default.

rules.source: Gopen & Swan, The Science of Scientific Writing (1990); Williams & Bizup, Style

rules.name: Put conditions before instructions
rules.dont: Instructions that tell the reader to act and only then say when: "Clear the cache if it's full", "Run the migration, but only on staging".
rules.do: Put the condition first: "If the cache is full, clear it."
rules.rationale: A reader following steps acts as soon as they read the verb. If the condition comes last, they may already have done the wrong thing.
detect: Imperative verb at sentence start with 'if', 'unless', 'when', or 'only' later in the sentence

examples.bad: Clear the cache if it is full.
examples.better: If the cache is full, clear it.
examples.note: Human-identified: Google developer documentation style guide.

examples.bad: Delete the old branch unless someone else is using it.
examples.better: If the old branch is unused, delete it.

examples.bad: Run the migration, but only on staging.
examples.better: On staging only, run the migration.

rules.source: Google developer documentation style guide

rules.name: Use "must" for requirements
rules.dont: "Shall", "is required to", "it is mandatory that", and soft forms for real requirements ("you may want to", "you may be able to").
rules.do: Use "must" for requirements, "need to" for administrative steps, "can" for options, and "must not" for prohibitions.
rules.rationale: "Shall" is ambiguous even in law (it can mean must, may, or will). GOV.UK and the federal guidelines both standardize on must / need / can.
detect: shall / shall not
'is required to', 'it is mandatory'
'you may be able to' for a plain option
rules.exceptions: Keep "shall" when quoting a statute or contract verbatim.

examples.bad: The applicant shall submit Form 12 within 30 days.
examples.better: You must submit Form 12 within 30 days.

examples.bad: You may be able to claim a refund.
examples.better: You can claim a refund.

examples.bad: Contributors are required to sign the CLA.
examples.better: You must sign the CLA before we can merge your pull request.

rules.source: Federal Plain Language Guidelines (plainlanguage.gov / digital.gov); GOV.UK style guide

rules.name: Say it positively
rules.dont: Negative and double-negative constructions the reader has to flip: "not uncommon", "may not ... unless", "no X other than", "persons other than ... may not".
rules.do: State what is true or what the reader can do.
rules.rationale: Each negation is a small logic step for the reader. Two in one sentence invite misreading.
detect: not + un-/in-/non- word
A negative plus 'unless', 'except', or 'other than' in one clause
Two negatives in one sentence
HHS 2.4: use 'don't' sparingly and avoid 'should', which reads as preachy
rules.exceptions: Warnings that must stand out ("Do not unplug during the update") are fine. usability.gov 15:10: a negative can be clearer when a wrong step is likely or its consequences are serious. 'You should' is fine for genuine recommendations in technical advice; the HHS caution is about preaching to the reader.

examples.bad: Persons other than the primary beneficiary may not receive these dividends.
examples.better: Only the primary beneficiary may receive these dividends.

examples.bad: This error is not uncommon when the cache is cold.
examples.better: This error is common when the cache is cold.

examples.bad: You cannot deploy without approval unless it's a hotfix.
examples.better: You need approval to deploy, except for hotfixes.

examples.bad: You can't deploy without running the migrations.
examples.better: Run the migrations before you deploy.
examples.note: Negative instruction turned into a positive step.

examples.bad: Do not ride your bicycle without wearing a helmet.
examples.better: Wear your helmet every time you ride your bicycle.
examples.note: Human-identified: CDC Simply Put; also HHS Health Literacy Online 2.4.

rules.source: SEC Plain English Handbook (1998); Williams & Bizup, Style; Federal Plain Language Guidelines (plainlanguage.gov / digital.gov); Google developer documentation style guide; HHS Health Literacy Online (2016); CDC Simply Put; Mailchimp Content Style Guide; Research-Based Web Design & Usability Guidelines (usability.gov), ch. 15

rules.name: Climb down the ladder of abstraction
rules.dont: Abstract category words where a concrete one exists: aspects, factors, elements, issues, considerations, matters, facets, dimensions, things; and "asset" when you mean "one share of IBM stock".
rules.do: Name the most specific thing that is still true: the file, the number, the person, the error message.
rules.rationale: Concrete words create a picture the reader can check. Abstract ones make the reader guess which instance you mean. The SEC handbook illustrates this with a ladder from "asset" down to "one share of IBM common stock".
detect: '[aspect/factor/element/issue/consideration] of' with no concrete noun nearby
A sentence a reader couldn't picture or test
rules.exceptions: Abstract words are fine in a summary that the next sentences make concrete.

examples.bad: There are various factors to consider regarding the performance aspects of this approach.
examples.better: This approach adds a database query to every page load, about 30 ms.

examples.bad: Investors should consider their assets.
examples.better: Check how many shares of IBM common stock you own.
examples.note: Built from the SEC handbook's ladder of abstraction.

examples.bad: We addressed several key issues.
examples.better: We fixed the login timeout and the duplicate email bug.

rules.source: SEC Plain English Handbook (1998); Orwell, Politics and the English Language (1946); Pinker, The Sense of Style (2014); Strunk & White

rules.name: Use the short, familiar word
rules.dont: Formal words where an everyday one means the same: purchase, assist, approximately, commence, initiate, modify, execute (a program), terminate, sufficient, additional, numerous, prior to, subsequent to, in excess of, with regard to, in accordance with, endeavor, ascertain, demonstrate, obtain, require, regarding, per annum, e.g., i.e. The federal guidelines' 'dirty dozen' are: addressees, assist/assistance, commence, implement, in accordance with, in order that, in the amount of, in the event of, it is, promulgate, this activity/command, utilize/utilization.
rules.do: Use the plain word: buy, help, about, start, change, run, end, enough, more, many, before, after, more than, about, under, try, find out, show, get, need, about, a year, for example, that is.
rules.rationale: Orwell's second rule, GOV.UK, 18F, and Google all say this. In Oppenheimer's experiments, readers rated writers who used needlessly long words as less intelligent.
detect: Any listed word where the plain one carries the same meaning
rules.exceptions: Use the formal word when it's the precise term in your field ("terminate a process", "execute a contract"). 'Implement' is the precise word for code (implement an interface); the federal list targets the bureaucratic sense.

examples.bad: Please assist the customer in obtaining approximately 3 additional licenses prior to the commencement of the trial.
examples.better: Help the customer get about 3 more licenses before the trial starts.

examples.bad: Purchase approximately 10 units.
examples.better: Buy about 10 units.

examples.bad: Subsequent to modification of the settings, terminate and reinitiate the service.
examples.better: After you change the settings, restart the service.

examples.bad: If there are any points on which you require explanation or further particulars we shall be glad to furnish such additional details as may be required by telephone.
examples.better: If you have any questions, please phone.
examples.note: Human-identified: Plain English Campaign before-and-after examples.

examples.bad: High-quality learning environments are a necessary precondition for facilitation and enhancement of the ongoing learning process.
examples.better: Children need good schools if they are to learn properly.
examples.note: Human-identified: Plain English Campaign before-and-after examples.

rules.source: Orwell, Politics and the English Language (1946); GOV.UK style guide; 18F content guide; Google developer documentation style guide; Oppenheimer, Applied Cognitive Psychology (2006); Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011), via plainlanguage.gov archive; CDC Everyday Words for Public Health Communication; Microsoft Writing Style Guide; CDC Clear Communication Index; CDC Simply Put; Flesch, How to Write Plain English

rules.name: Define terms and abbreviations the first time
rules.dont: Unexplained acronyms, internal codenames, and specialist terms used as if the reader knows them.
rules.do: Spell out an abbreviation at first use, with the short form in parentheses. Explain a specialist term in plain words the first time, or use the plain words instead.
rules.rationale: Undefined terms are the most visible symptom of the curse of knowledge. GOV.UK requires explaining specialist terms even for specialist audiences.
detect: Three or more undefined acronyms in one sentence (pattern); any acronym not defined earlier (LLM check)
Internal project names or ticket codes with no explanation
HHS 2.6: define a term in context the first time; don't rely on a glossary or hover text
Simply Put: for a familiar acronym write HIV (human immunodeficiency virus); for an unfamiliar one write sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS)
usability.gov 15:4-15:5: use abbreviations only when much shorter and widely understood
rules.exceptions: Abbreviations your reader uses daily (API, URL) don't need defining.

examples.bad: Per the TPS process, file an RFE with the ARB before EOD.
examples.better: Ask the architecture review board for an exception by 5 p.m. today.

examples.bad: ICSs will deliver their core purpose.
examples.better: Integrated care systems (local NHS partnerships) will run local health services.
examples.note: Built from a 2021 Golden Bull winner.

examples.bad: Make sure DLQ depth stays low.
examples.better: Make sure few messages pile up in the dead-letter queue (DLQ), where failed messages go.

examples.bad: Your primary doctor may refer you to a neurologist.
examples.better: Your primary doctor may refer you to a neurologist. A neurologist is a doctor who treats problems related to the brain and nervous system.

rules.source: GOV.UK style guide; Google developer documentation style guide; Pinker, The Sense of Style (2014); Federal Plain Language Guidelines (plainlanguage.gov / digital.gov); HHS Health Literacy Online (2016); CDC Simply Put; Mailchimp Content Style Guide; Research-Based Web Design & Usability Guidelines (usability.gov), ch. 15; CDC Clear Communication Index

rules.name: Give an example for every abstract claim
rules.dont: General statements left in the air: a principle, a pattern, or a definition with no instance the reader can picture.
rules.do: Follow the claim with one concrete example: a specific input and output, a real sentence, a number, or a case.
rules.rationale: Pinker's diagnosis of a journal sentence about stimulus timing: the experiment was simple (taps on the wrist, elbow, and shoulder feel like a hop), but the authors never said so. Examples let readers check the claim.
detect: A paragraph of claims with no instance, number, or quoted case
A definition with no example

examples.bad: Caching can introduce consistency issues in distributed systems.
examples.better: Caching can show stale data. For example, a user changes their email, but the profile page shows the old one for 60 seconds.

examples.bad: (A journal sentence describing 'stimulus' and 'poststimulus events' in the abstract.)
examples.better: Tap someone's wrist, then elbow, then shoulder. They feel one tap hopping up the arm.
examples.note: Pinker's rabbit-illusion example in The Sense of Style. Described, not quoted.

rules.source: Pinker, The Sense of Style (2014); Sword, Zombie Nouns (NYT, 2012)

rules.name: Use present tense
rules.dont: Future and conditional tenses for things that are simply true: "will return", "would display", "will be shown".
rules.do: Describe behavior in the present: "returns", "shows".
rules.rationale: Present tense is the simplest verb form, and conditionals make readers ask 'would, if what?'
detect: will/would + verb describing ordinary behavior in docs or UI text
rules.exceptions: Use future tense for real future events ("The API will be retired on June 1").

examples.bad: These sections describe types of information that would satisfy the application requirements of Circular A-110 as it would apply to this grant program.
examples.better: These sections tell you how to meet the requirements of Circular A-110 for this grant program.

examples.bad: Clicking Save will display a confirmation message.
examples.better: When you click Save, a confirmation message appears.

examples.bad: The function would return null if the key is missing.
examples.better: The function returns null if the key is missing.

rules.source: Federal Plain Language Guidelines (plainlanguage.gov / digital.gov); Google developer documentation style guide

rules.name: Number steps, one action per step
rules.dont: Procedures written as paragraphs ("First, ... Then, ... After that, ... Finally, ..."), and steps that bundle several actions.
rules.do: Use a numbered list for steps that happen in order. Give each step one action, starting with the verb.
rules.rationale: Readers carry out procedures one step at a time and need to find their place again. Google and the federal guidelines both call for numbered lists here.
detect: Sequence words (first, then, next, after that, finally) chained across sentences in prose
A numbered step with two or more 'and then' actions
STE: one instruction per sentence; usability.gov 15:1: present steps in their natural order
rules.exceptions: A two-step sequence reads fine as one sentence.

examples.bad: First, open the settings. Then, find the API section. After that, copy the key. Finally, paste it into .env.
examples.better:
1. Open Settings.
2. In the API section, copy the key.
3. Paste the key into .env.

examples.bad: 3. Install the CLI and log in and then run init.
examples.better:
3. Install the CLI.
4. Log in.
5. Run init.

rules.source: Google developer documentation style guide; Federal Plain Language Guidelines (plainlanguage.gov / digital.gov); Microsoft Writing Style Guide; ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English (via Wikipedia); Research-Based Web Design & Usability Guidelines (usability.gov), ch. 15; NIH/NCI Clear & Simple

rules.name: Make list items parallel
rules.dont: Lists that mix forms: a verb phrase, then a noun, then a full sentence; mixed capitalization or end punctuation.
rules.do: Start every item the same way (all verbs, or all nouns) and punctuate them the same way.
rules.rationale: Parallel items let the reader compare them at a glance. Mixed forms make each item a new parsing job.
detect: List items that start with different parts of speech
Some items end with periods and others don't

examples.bad:
- Install dependencies
- Configuration of the database
- You should run the tests.
examples.better:
- Install dependencies.
- Configure the database.
- Run the tests.

examples.bad: Benefits: faster builds, it's cheaper, and having fewer flaky tests.
examples.better: Benefits: faster builds, lower cost, and fewer flaky tests.

rules.source: Google developer documentation style guide; Microsoft Writing Style Guide; Federal Plain Language Guidelines (plainlanguage.gov / digital.gov)

rules.name: Avoid idioms and culture-bound references
rules.dont: Idioms that don't translate or that some readers won't know: back burner, ballpark, boil the ocean, ducks in a row, hit the ground running, move the goalposts, piece of cake, silver bullet, bite the bullet, in the weeds, drink from a firehose, home run, slam dunk, Hail Mary; and seasons or holidays as dates.
rules.do: Say the literal meaning: later, rough estimate, try to do everything, prepared, start quickly, change the requirements, easy, single fix, accept the cost, deep in the details.
rules.rationale: Idioms fail for readers with limited English and in translation. Google's global-audience guide and 18F both rule them out.
detect: Any listed idiom
'this summer', 'by Thanksgiving' as a deadline
rules.exceptions: Fine in casual internal chat with people who share the idiom.

examples.bad: Let's put this on the back burner and get a ballpark figure.
examples.better: Let's pause this and get a rough estimate.

examples.bad: There's no silver bullet; we'll have to bite the bullet and rewrite it.
examples.better: No single fix will work. We need to rewrite the module.

examples.bad: We'll ship it this summer.
examples.better: We'll ship it by August 31.

rules.source: Google developer documentation style guide; 18F content guide; Orwell, Politics and the English Language (1946); Mailchimp Content Style Guide; Microsoft Writing Style Guide

rules.name: Keep paragraphs to one idea
rules.dont: Paragraphs that cover several topics or run past five or six sentences.
rules.do: Give each paragraph one idea, stated early. Start a new paragraph when the topic changes.
rules.rationale: GOV.UK caps paragraphs at five sentences. The federal guidelines recommend no more than 150 words in three to eight sentences, never over 250, and say an occasional one-sentence paragraph is fine. In Morkes and Nielsen's 1997 studies, several users read only the first sentence of each paragraph while scanning. Their concise and scannable versions scored 58% and 47% better on overall usability.
detect: Six or more sentences in one paragraph
Two unrelated topics in one paragraph
Over 150 words (warn) or 250 words (always split), per the federal guidelines
Paragraph targets by source: HHS 3 lines or fewer on the web; Simply Put 3-5 sentences; usability.gov and STE 6 or fewer; federal guidelines 150 words
usability.gov 15:11: the first sentence should state the paragraph's topic and scope, because readers skim the first one or two sentences
rules.exceptions: Narrative and argument can run longer when each sentence builds on the last.

examples.bad: The build is slow. It takes 12 minutes. Most of that is tests. Also, the docs are out of date. Someone should update the README. And we need a new logo.
examples.better:
The build takes 12 minutes, and most of that time is tests.

Separately, the README is out of date.

examples.bad: I fixed the login bug. The fix changes how tokens refresh. Separately, the deploy moved to Thursday. Also, Priya starts Monday. She needs a laptop. I ordered one yesterday.
examples.better:
I fixed the login bug. The fix changes how tokens refresh.

The deploy moved to Thursday.

Priya starts Monday, and I ordered her laptop yesterday.

rules.source: GOV.UK style guide; Nielsen & Morkes, NN/g (1997); Williams & Bizup, Style; Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011), via plainlanguage.gov archive; HHS Health Literacy Online (2016); CDC Simply Put; Research-Based Web Design & Usability Guidelines (usability.gov), ch. 15; ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English (via Wikipedia)

rules.name: Keep only what the reader needs
rules.dont: Background, history, statistics, and nice-to-know details placed before or around the action, and pieces that try to cover every angle.
rules.do: Separate need-to-know from nice-to-know and cut the rest, or link to it. Limit a section to three or four main ideas.
rules.rationale: HHS found many users want just the basics: 'Just tell me what I need to know.' NIH's Clear & Simple says to separate what readers need to know from what they want to know and what you want to tell them, and to cut the last two.
detect: Background or history before the action the reader came for
More than three or four main ideas in one section
Statistics that don't change what the reader will do
rules.exceptions: Reference documentation can be comprehensive; put the summary first.

examples.bad: (Three paragraphs on the history of the feature, then: 'To turn it on, open Settings.')
examples.better: To turn it on, open Settings > Features. (History is in the changelog.)

examples.bad: Blood pressure is the force of blood against the artery walls. It is measured in millimeters of mercury. Normal is below 120/80. Check it often.
examples.better: Check your blood pressure every 2 years, especially if you're 40 or older.

rules.source: HHS Health Literacy Online (2016); NIH/NCI Clear & Simple; CDC Simply Put; Mailchimp Content Style Guide

rules.name: Say what to do, how, and why
rules.dont: Text that informs but never says what the reader should do, or names an action without the steps or the reason.
rules.do: Give at least one specific action. Break it into small steps, and say why each step matters and what the reader gains.
rules.rationale: CDC's Clear Communication Index scores a call to action, an explanation of why the behavior matters, and directions for how to do it (items 5, 12-14). HHS found users want steps they can take right away, and explaining the 'why' and the benefit motivates action.
detect: No imperative or 'you can' action in a message meant to prompt action
An action with no how-to steps
A step with no reason
rules.exceptions: Purely informational answers (a definition, a status report) need no call to action.

examples.bad: Following safety precautions can reduce food-borne disease transmission.
examples.better: Cook meat until it's no longer pink in the middle. Wash raw fruit and vegetables before you eat them.

examples.bad: Keep a food diary.
examples.better: Keep a food diary. Knowing what you eat now helps you decide what to change.
examples.note: Human-identified: HHS Health Literacy Online 2.5: explain the why.

examples.bad: The deployment failed due to a config mismatch.
examples.better: The deployment failed because staging.env is missing DATABASE_URL. Add it, then run make deploy again.

rules.source: CDC Clear Communication Index; HHS Health Literacy Online (2016); CDC Simply Put; NIH/NCI Clear & Simple

rules.name: Make numbers easy to use
rules.dont: Numbers the reader has to decode or compute: decimals and percentages where a whole number or 'X out of Y' works, relative risk without a baseline, numbers with no context, and words like 'high' or 'small' with no number.
rules.do: Use whole numbers or natural frequencies ('8 out of 10'), say what the number means (high or low, more or less than expected), do the math for the reader, and keep denominators the same when comparing.
rules.rationale: CDC's Clear Communication Index items 15-17 and 20: readers understand natural frequencies better than percentages, and absolute risk better than relative risk. Simply Put suggests leading with a general word and putting the statistic in parentheses.
detect: Percent or decimal where a natural frequency would do
'X% more likely' with no baseline
'high', 'low', 'small', 'significant' with no number
A comparison that makes the reader divide or convert
rules.exceptions: Technical audiences reading benchmarks or financial data may need exact decimals.

examples.bad: Taking the drug makes a stroke 50% less likely.
examples.better: Without the drug, 2 out of 100 people like you have a stroke. With it, 1 out of 100 does.

examples.bad: 90% of Americans believe vaccines are safe.
examples.better: Almost all Americans (90%) believe vaccines are safe.
examples.note: Human-identified: CDC Simply Put: general word first, number in parentheses.

examples.bad: The error rate is high.
examples.better: The error rate is 4%, up from 0.5% last week.

examples.bad: Feel for lumps about 5 to 6 millimeters in diameter.
examples.better: Feel for lumps about the size of a pea.
examples.note: Human-identified: CDC Simply Put: a familiar comparison instead of a measurement.

rules.source: CDC Clear Communication Index; CDC Simply Put

rules.name: Say what is known and what isn't
rules.dont: Presenting uncertain findings as settled, or hiding the limits of a result.
rules.do: State what you know, what you don't, and what could change the answer, with the specific reason. Keep it to one sentence where possible.
rules.rationale: CDC's Clear Communication Index item 11 asks that materials acknowledge uncertainty and that guidance may change. This is the honest counterpart to FILL-04 and FILL-06, which cut reflexive hedges and generic disclaimers.
detect: A conclusion with no stated basis or limit
A recommendation from incomplete data with no note that it may change
rules.exceptions: Don't stack hedges (FILL-04) or add vague disclaimers (FILL-06); name the specific unknown.

examples.bad: The fix resolves the memory leak.
examples.better: The fix stopped the leak in a 6-hour soak test. I haven't tested the 48-hour job, where it first appeared.

examples.bad: This vaccine prevents the new variant.
examples.better: In the first 2 published studies, people who got the vaccine had less severe illness from the new variant. We'll update this page as more data come in.

rules.source: CDC Clear Communication Index

rules.name: Write link text that says where it goes
rules.dont: Links on 'click here', 'here', 'this', 'read more', or 'learn more', and bare URLs in running prose.
rules.do: Link the words that name the destination or action: 'Read the [setup guide]'.
rules.rationale: Screen-reader users often browse a list of links out of context, and every reader scans link text. Mailchimp, Google, and HHS all require descriptive links.
detect: Link text of click here / here / this / read more / learn more / more / link

examples.bad: For setup steps, [click here](https://example.org/setup).
examples.better: See the [setup guide](https://example.org/setup).

examples.bad: Learn more about pricing [here](https://example.org/pricing).
examples.better: Compare [plans and pricing](https://example.org/pricing).

rules.source: Mailchimp Content Style Guide; Google developer documentation style guide; HHS Health Literacy Online (2016)

rules.name: Don't depend on position, color, or images
rules.dont: Instructions that only work if the reader sees the layout: 'above', 'below', 'in the right sidebar', 'the green button', 'see the screenshot'.
rules.do: Name the thing by its label and give the steps in text. Use numbered steps and visible labels.
rules.rationale: Layouts change on mobile, colors don't reach color-blind or screen-reader users, and images may not load. Mailchimp and Google both ban directional language in instructions.
detect: above/below/left/right/sidebar as the only locator
color as the only identifier
'see the image' with no text equivalent
rules.exceptions: 'Below' is fine for a document's own structure in print, such as 'the table below' when the table follows immediately.

examples.bad: Choose a plan from the left-hand panel.
examples.better:
Choose one of these plans:
1. Free
2. Pro
examples.note: The panel may not be on the left on a phone or in a screen reader.

examples.bad: Click the green button.
examples.better: Click Save.

rules.source: Mailchimp Content Style Guide; Google developer documentation style guide; HHS Health Literacy Online (2016)

rules.name: Choose words with one meaning
rules.dont: Words that can be read two ways: 'since' (time or because), 'once' (one time or after), 'right' (correct or direction), 'while' (time or although), and nouns that are also verbs (file, report, record, screen) where the role is unclear.
rules.do: Use the unambiguous word: because, after, correct, although.
rules.rationale: Microsoft and Mailchimp both flag these words for global readers and translation. Simply Put asks for words with a single clear meaning.
detect: Sentence-initial 'Since' meaning 'because'
'Once' meaning 'after'
'right' meaning 'correct'
rules.exceptions: 'Since' is fine for time ('since 2019'); 'once' for a single occurrence.

examples.bad: Since you created the table, you can change it.
examples.better: Because you created the table, you can change it.

examples.bad: Once the job finishes, deploy.
examples.better: After the job finishes, deploy.
examples.note: 'Once' can mean 'one time' or 'after'. Mailchimp's translation guidance and Microsoft's global-writing tips both flag it.

examples.bad: Make sure the setting is right.
examples.better: Make sure the setting is correct.

rules.source: Microsoft Writing Style Guide; Mailchimp Content Style Guide; CDC Simply Put

rules.name: Make the actor the subject
rules.dont: Sentences whose subject is an abstract noun (request, decision, attempt) while the real actor hides in a possessive or a prepositional phrase.
rules.do: Put the person or thing that acts in the subject slot, and the action in the verb.
rules.rationale: A sentence is a small story. It reads fastest when the character is the subject and the action is the verb (Williams).
detect: Subject is an abstract noun while a person or component is the real actor
Actor appears only as a possessive (the duck's arrival) or after 'by'
Passive with a by-phrase: the actor is named but not in the subject slot
rules.exceptions: Fine when the sentence is really about the object and the actor is known ("The report is due Friday").

examples.bad: A request for grapes was made upon the duck's arrival at the lemonade stand.
examples.better: A duck walked up to a lemonade stand and asked for grapes.

examples.bad: The decision to drop the Redis cache was driven by latency concerns.
examples.better: I dropped the Redis cache because it slowed down requests.

examples.bad: A determination was made that the migration is safe to run.
examples.better: I checked the migration, and it's safe to run.

examples.bad: An attempt to reproduce the bug on main was unsuccessful.
examples.better: I couldn't reproduce the bug on main.

examples.bad: The lake was polluted by the company.
examples.better: The company polluted the lake.

examples.bad: The stock is bought by the investor.
examples.better: The investor buys the stock.

examples.bad: Heart disease and lung cancer are caused by smoking.
examples.better: Smoking causes heart disease and lung cancer.

rules.source: zonderlabs.com/slop + x.com/zhizdev thread; Williams & Bizup, Style; Gopen & Swan, The Science of Scientific Writing (1990); Federal Plain Language Guidelines (plainlanguage.gov / digital.gov)

rules.name: Use verbs, not nominalizations
rules.dont: Actions buried in nouns (investigation, reduction, completion, verification), usually carried by an empty verb (make, perform, conduct, provide, do, carry out).
rules.do: Turn the noun back into a verb and drop the empty verb.
rules.rationale: Nominalizations make the reader rebuild the action, and they usually delete the actor.
detect: Light verb + article + -tion/-ment/-ance/-ence/-al/-sis noun
"X of the Y" where X is a nominalized verb
rules.exceptions: Keep a nominalization that names an established thing ("the migration", "authentication") rather than an action. Sword: at their best, nominalizations name complex ideas (perception, epistemology). Linguists at Language Log note the real fault is needless length and a hidden actor, not the suffix itself.

examples.bad: I did an investigation of the failing test.
examples.better: I investigated the failing test.

examples.bad: This change provides a reduction in memory usage.
examples.better: This change cuts memory use.

examples.bad: Completion of the migration is pending confirmation from you.
examples.better: I'll finish the migration once you confirm.

examples.bad: I performed a verification of the fix against staging.
examples.better: I tested the fix on staging.

examples.bad: We conduct an analysis of the data.
examples.better: We analyze data.

examples.bad: We are responsible for management of the program.
examples.better: We manage the program.

examples.bad: We will have no stock ownership of the company.
examples.better: We will not own the company's stock.

rules.source: zonderlabs.com/slop + x.com/zhizdev thread; Sword, Zombie Nouns (NYT, 2012); SEC Plain English Handbook (1998); Federal Plain Language Guidelines (plainlanguage.gov / digital.gov); Williams & Bizup, Style

rules.name: Say who did it
rules.dont: Agentless passives for actions with a known actor: "was updated", "were run", "mistakes were made", "it is believed that".
rules.do: Name the actor (I, you, the script, the team, commit a1b2c3) and put it first.
rules.rationale: The passive hides whether Claude, the user, or a script made the change, and the reader needs that to trust the claim.
detect: be-verb + past participle with no 'by' phrase where the actor is known
Status reports made entirely of passives
"It is believed/thought/considered that"
rules.exceptions: Use the passive when the actor is unknown or irrelevant ("The package was deprecated in 2023"), in error messages, or to keep a topic in subject position across sentences. GOV.UK also accepts the passive when the outcome matters more than the actor. Check that it really is passive: Pullum showed that Strunk & White misidentified three of their four 'passive' examples.

examples.bad: The config file was updated and the tests were run.
examples.better: I updated config.ts and ran the tests. All 42 pass.

examples.bad: The bug has been fixed.
examples.better: I fixed the bug in parseDate. It now handles time zones.

examples.bad: It is believed that the endpoint is deprecated.
examples.better: The API docs mark this endpoint as deprecated.

examples.bad: Changes were made to the auth flow to address the issue.
examples.better: I changed the login handler so expired tokens redirect to sign-in.

examples.bad: The following information must be included in the application for it to be considered complete.
examples.better: You must include the following information in your application.

examples.bad: An electronic travel authorisation is needed.
examples.better: You need an electronic travel authorisation.

examples.bad: Tests may be needed to find out what's wrong.
examples.better: You may need a test to find out what's wrong.

rules.source: zonderlabs.com/slop + x.com/zhizdev thread; Declaude (danielrosehill/Declaude); stop-slop (hardikpandya/stop-slop); Federal Plain Language Guidelines (plainlanguage.gov / digital.gov); GOV.UK style guide; Army Regulation 25-50 (BLUF); SEC Plain English Handbook (1998); HHS Health Literacy Online (2016); CDC Simply Put; Mailchimp Content Style Guide; Research-Based Web Design & Usability Guidelines (usability.gov), ch. 15

rules.name: Don't let abstractions act
rules.dont: Abstract nouns or inanimate things doing human things: "this change ensures", "the data tells us", "the decision emerged", "a complaint becomes a fix", "the culture shifts", "that gives us a vehicle".
rules.do: Name the concrete thing and what it does, or name the person who acted.
rules.rationale: False agency sounds like an action but says nothing checkable, and it avoids naming who did the work.
detect: Subject is this/that/the change/fix/approach/data/result/decision/market/culture with a human verb (ensures, unlocks, tells, emerges, rewards, settles, becomes)
rules.exceptions: Standard technical phrasing is fine when literal ("the function returns null", "the test fails").

examples.bad: This refactor unlocks a cleaner seam for future work.
examples.better: You can now add a payment provider without editing the router.

examples.bad: The data tells us users prefer the old layout.
examples.better: In the A/B test, 61% of users switched back to the old layout.

examples.bad: What this settles. Nothing was wrong with CUDA.
examples.better: The slowdown came from the kernel design. CUDA itself was fine.
examples.note: From the zonderlabs Claude Code sample.

examples.bad: Within a week, the complaint became a fix.
examples.better: The team fixed it within a week of the complaint.

rules.source: zonderlabs.com/slop + x.com/zhizdev thread; stop-slop (hardikpandya/stop-slop)

rules.name: Use "is" and "has"
rules.dont: Fancy stand-ins for is/are/has: serves as, stands as, functions as, acts as, represents, marks, boasts, features, offers, maintains, refers to.
rules.do: Use "is", "are", or "has" unless the fancier verb adds real meaning.
rules.rationale: LLM text measurably avoids plain copulas. The substitutes add a promotional tone and no information.
detect: serves/stands/functions/acts as + noun phrase
boasts/features/offers where 'has' fits
"X refers to" in a sentence about X itself
rules.exceptions: "Represents" is fine for literal representation (a variable represents a value). "Features" is fine as a noun.

examples.bad: Gallery 825 serves as the association's exhibition space. The gallery features four separate rooms.
examples.better: Gallery 825 is the association's exhibition space. It has four rooms.

examples.bad: The utils module serves as the central hub for shared helpers.
examples.better: The utils module holds the shared helpers.

examples.bad: The new release boasts improved startup time.
examples.better: The new release starts about 30% faster.

examples.bad: This endpoint functions as a health check.
examples.better: This endpoint is a health check.

rules.source: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; Humanizer (blader/humanizer)

rules.name: State relationships directly
rules.dont: Vague links between subjects: "associated with", "connected to", "in connection with", and stiff source framing like "records identify him as", "his profile lists".
rules.do: Say the actual relationship with a plain verb: worked at, wrote, owns, calls, depends on.
rules.rationale: "Associated with" hides what the relationship is. The reader can't tell whether X built, owns, uses, or merely appears near Y.
detect: associated/connected with or to, in connection with
[source] identifies/lists/records [subject] as
rules.exceptions: "Associated" is fine as a technical term (an associated type, a file association).

examples.bad: In 2017, Jane Doe was associated with the leadership of ExampleCorp.
examples.better: In 2017, Jane Doe was CEO of ExampleCorp.

examples.bad: The failures appear connected to the cache layer.
examples.better: The failures happen only when the cache returns a stale entry.

examples.bad: His parliamentary biography records that he served as president of the club.
examples.better: He was president of the club.

rules.source: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing

rules.name: Break up noun stacks
rules.dont: Three or more nouns, or chains of hyphenated modifiers, packed into one phrase: "user-session entry boundary", "grape availability request", "vision-and-transcript pass".
rules.do: Unpack the stack into a clause with a verb and prepositions.
rules.rationale: Stacked nouns hide how the words relate. This was the most common fault in Claude Code replies.
detect: 3+ nouns in a row acting as one phrase
Hyphenated compound modifiers stacked before a noun
Possessive on an abstract noun (a label's awareness entry)
Google's limit: no more than two nouns stacked before another noun
STE caps multi-word nouns at three words; Google at two nouns before a noun; Microsoft: avoid modifier stacks
rules.exceptions: Established compounds are fine ("database connection pool", "pull request").

examples.bad: The database readiness check sits at the user-session entry boundary, before the authentication handler runs.
examples.better: When a user's session starts, we check that the database is ready. This happens before authentication.

examples.bad: The length floor drops a block.
examples.better: If a section is shorter than the minimum length, it gets removed.
examples.note: Source example. Meaning is a guess.

examples.bad: I added a vision-and-transcript pass.
examples.better: I added a step that checks both the video frames and the transcript.

examples.bad: This is a label's awareness entry.
examples.better: This entry records which labels the model knows about.
examples.note: Source example. Meaning is a guess.

examples.bad: With an extremely well thought-out Windows migration project plan, your migration will go more smoothly.
examples.better: Your migration will go more smoothly if you have a project plan that's well thought out.
examples.note: Human-identified: Microsoft Writing Style Guide, global writing tips.

rules.source: zonderlabs.com/slop + x.com/zhizdev thread; Humanizer (blader/humanizer); Google developer documentation style guide; Microsoft Writing Style Guide; ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English (via Wikipedia)

rules.name: Call things by their ordinary name
rules.dont: Categories, inflated verbs, and formal synonyms in place of the plain word: beverage retailer, compute substrate, utilize, leverage, facilitate, persistence layer, invocation site.
rules.do: Use the word a colleague would use: lemonade stand, GPU, use, help, the database, where it's called.
rules.rationale: The source names this as the AI-specific failure: word combinations no person would choose.
detect: Category word where the specific thing is known
Inflated verbs (utilize, leverage, facilitate, optimize, empower)
GOV.UK: use the words your users search for ('lorry', not 'heavy goods vehicle')
rules.exceptions: Use the formal term when it's the precise one and the reader knows it ("leverage" in finance).

examples.bad: The duck made a grape availability request as he arrived at the beverage retailer.
examples.better: The duck walked up to the lemonade stand and asked if they had grapes.

examples.bad: We leverage the persistence layer to facilitate session continuity.
examples.better: We store sessions in Postgres so users stay logged in.

examples.bad: I utilized the compute substrate more efficiently.
examples.better: The job now uses the GPU more efficiently.

examples.bad: The invocation site passes a null config.
examples.better: The code that calls loadConfig passes null.

examples.bad: The cognitive process that staff will go through when interpreting prescriptions and selecting drugs is almost intuitive.
examples.better: Our pharmacists know the drugs well, so they read prescriptions quickly.
examples.note: Human-identified: Plain English Campaign Golden Bull, 2003 (Lloyds pharmacy). Rewrite is ours.

rules.source: zonderlabs.com/slop + x.com/zhizdev thread; Declaude (danielrosehill/Declaude); Humanizer (blader/humanizer); Orwell, Politics and the English Language (1946); GOV.UK style guide; 18F content guide

rules.name: Don't coin terms the reader hasn't seen
rules.dont: Invented labels used as if the reader knows them: "the warm regime", "fat-CTA design", "CUDA-only knobs", "the ruler", "lab-check".
rules.do: Say the plain thing, or define the term once the first time you use it.
rules.rationale: Coined labels make sense to the writer, who has the context. The reader has to reverse-engineer them.
detect: A noun phrase introduced with 'the' as if already known
Hyphenated coinages
Metaphor used as a technical term
rules.exceptions: Fine when the term is defined in the same reply or is standard in the user's codebase.

examples.bad: The ruler is a floor, and the report should say so.
examples.better: The benchmark gives only a lower bound on errors. The report should say that.

examples.bad: The first CUDA-only knobs already buy 3 to 5% on qkv.
examples.better: Two settings that only CUDA exposes already make the qkv kernel 3% to 5% faster.

examples.bad: The one remaining warm-regime gap is purely stage depth.
examples.better: On repeated runs, one kernel is still slower. The cause is the number of pipeline stages.

examples.bad: Next: lab-check it on the H200.
examples.better: Next, I'll test it on the H200.

rules.source: zonderlabs.com/slop + x.com/zhizdev thread

rules.name: Make every pointer word resolvable
rules.dont: "It", "this", "that", "the issue", "the gap" with no single clear referent in the previous sentence.
rules.do: Repeat the noun, or rewrite so the referent is obvious.
rules.rationale: Ambiguous references force the reader to scroll back and guess.
detect: Sentence starts with This/That/It + verb and the previous sentence has several candidates
"the issue/problem/gap" with no earlier mention
rules.exceptions: "This" is fine when the previous sentence has one obvious referent.

examples.bad: I updated the retry logic and the timeout. This should fix it.
examples.better: Raising the timeout to 30 seconds should fix the flaky upload test.

examples.bad: That covers the main case. The other one needs more work.
examples.better: The fix handles logged-in users, but guest checkout still fails.
examples.note: Comma restored: 'but' joins two independent clauses (see FMT-13).

examples.bad: The gap is real but modest.
examples.better: Claude's error rate is higher than the human rate but only slightly.

examples.bad: Make sure that it's targeted.
examples.better: Make sure that the ad is targeted.
examples.note: Human-identified: Google developer documentation style guide.

rules.source: zonderlabs.com/slop + x.com/zhizdev thread; Google developer documentation style guide; Mailchimp Content Style Guide; Microsoft Writing Style Guide

rules.name: State technical claims literally
rules.dont: Metaphors standing in for technical claims: a setting "buys" speed, a check "sits at" a boundary, a result "tells a story", a fix "closes the gap".
rules.do: Say the literal claim with the number or mechanism.
rules.rationale: Metaphors make the reader translate back to the literal claim, and the translation can go wrong.
detect: Economic verbs for performance (buys, costs, pays for)
Spatial verbs for code flow (sits at, lives in, surfaces)
Narrative words for data (story, shape, picture)
Orwell's 'dying metaphors' and GOV.UK/18F's figurative-verb list: drive, tackle, land, ring-fence, one-stop shop
rules.exceptions: Idioms engineers read literally are fine ("the fix landed in main").

examples.bad: The shape of the defects is the better story than the height of the bars.
examples.better: Which kinds of errors appear matters more than how many there are.

examples.bad: 8 or 9 stages will close it.
examples.better: Using 8 or 9 pipeline stages should make it as fast as the Triton version.

examples.bad: The validation sits at the API boundary.
examples.better: We validate input in the request handler, before it reaches the service layer.

examples.bad: This buys us about 20 ms.
examples.better: This saves about 20 ms per request.

rules.source: zonderlabs.com/slop + x.com/zhizdev thread; 18F content guide; Orwell, Politics and the English Language (1946); Google developer documentation style guide

rules.name: Replace AI-marker words
rules.dont: Words that mark text as machine-written even once (avoid-ai-writing Tier 1A): delve, tapestry, realm, paradigm, embark, beacon, testament to, robust, pivotal, underscore, meticulous, seamless, watershed moment, thriving, showcase, bustling, intricate, interplay, ever-evolving, enduring, daunting, landscape (metaphor), journey (metaphor), symphony/dance/orchestra of (metaphor), embrace (metaphor), load-bearing (metaphor). Also "Additionally," to open a sentence.
rules.do: Use the plain word (explore, area, start, shows, strong, important, careful, smooth, complex, lasting, hard), or replace the word with the fact that would justify it.
rules.rationale: These words are over-represented in LLM output by large margins (Wikipedia's era lists; Antislop's measured frequency lists). Readers who know the list stop trusting the text at the first hit.
detect: Any listed word in its figurative sense
Sentence-initial 'Additionally,'
Promotional adjectives live in WORD-10 and jargon in WORD-07; this rule covers the rest
rules.exceptions: Literal or technical senses are fine: robust statistics, an underscore character, a load-bearing wall, a journey in a travel log. Synonyms are not suspect by default.

examples.bad: Additionally, this robust solution showcases a seamless integration.
examples.better: It also works with the existing billing system without code changes.

examples.bad: Let's delve into the intricate interplay between the scheduler and the queue.
examples.better: The scheduler and the queue interact in two places: retries and backpressure.

examples.bad: This release marks the next step in our journey toward a more robust platform.
examples.better: This release adds retries to every outbound call.

examples.bad: The report underscores the pivotal role of caching, a testament to meticulous engineering.
examples.better: The report found caching cut page load time from 2.1 s to 0.6 s.

rules.source: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; Humanizer (blader/humanizer); Declaude (danielrosehill/Declaude); no-ai-slop (realrossmanngroup); avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon); Antislop (sam-paech)

rules.name: Cut business jargon
rules.dont: Corporate filler: circle back, touch base, reach out, move the needle, low-hanging fruit, going forward / moving forward, bandwidth (for time), actionable insights, best practices, value-add, end-to-end, deep dive, unpack, navigate (challenges), lean into, double down, game-changer, paradigm shift, synergy, holistic, on the same page, take it offline, at the end of the day. Plus the GOV.UK and 18F list: deliver (for abstract things), drive (for schemes), tackle, progress (as a verb), key (unless it unlocks something), impact (as a verb), dialogue, liaise, incentivize, ring-fence, slim down, one-stop shop, touchpoint, thought leader, transform. The Plain English Campaign's management-speak list adds: blue-sky thinking, pushing the envelope, take it to the next level, bring to the table, core competencies, be proactive not reactive. Mailchimp's word list adds: automagical, ninja, rockstar, wizard, unicorn (unless literal), crushing it, killing it, best-in-breed, rise and grind, disruptor, funnel, learnings.
rules.do: Use the plain verb or noun: follow up, contact, improve, easy wins, from now on, time, findings, explain, handle.
rules.rationale: Jargon signals effort without content and often hides who will do what.
detect: Any listed phrase
rules.exceptions: "End-to-end" is fine as a test type; "bandwidth" is fine for networks.

examples.bad: Let's circle back on this going forward once we have bandwidth.
examples.better: Let's revisit this next sprint.

examples.bad: I'll do a deep dive to unpack the low-hanging fruit.
examples.better: I'll look for the easy fixes first.

examples.bad: This is a game-changer that will move the needle on retention.
examples.better: The change should raise 30-day retention. I'll measure it after two weeks.

examples.bad: Feel free to reach out if you want to touch base.
examples.better: Message me if you want to talk it through.

examples.bad: increase the share of wallet opportunity through a new capital light and low risk operating model
examples.better: sell more to the customers we have, cheaply and with little risk
examples.note: Human-identified: Plain English Campaign Golden Bull, 2021 (boohoo). Rewrite paraphrases the Campaign's translation.

examples.bad: provider collaboratives will be a key component in enabling ICSs to deliver their core purpose
examples.better: groups of healthcare providers working together will help local health systems do their main job
examples.note: Human-identified: Plain English Campaign Golden Bull, 2021 (NHS England). Rewrite paraphrases the Campaign's translation.

rules.source: Declaude (danielrosehill/Declaude); stop-slop (hardikpandya/stop-slop); GOV.UK style guide; 18F content guide; Plain English Campaign; Plain English Campaign examples; Mailchimp Content Style Guide

rules.name: Cut intensifiers and softeners
rules.dont: Adverbs that add emphasis or sincerity but no meaning: really, very, just, literally, genuinely, honestly, simply, actually, deeply, truly, fundamentally, inherently, incredibly, extremely, absolutely, definitely, importantly, crucially, interestingly.
rules.do: Delete the adverb. If the sentence feels weak without it, replace the claim with a stronger fact.
rules.rationale: Intensifiers try to make a claim feel bigger; softeners try to make the writer seem sincere. Both read as filler.
detect: Any listed adverb
More than one -ly adverb per sentence
'the real/actual X' with no named fake X; moral adjectives on non-moral things ('honest caveat', 'honestly flagged')
rules.exceptions: Keep adverbs that carry information ("runs nightly", "fails intermittently"). "Just" meaning "only" or "a moment ago" is fine.

examples.bad: This is genuinely a really important fix.
examples.better: This fix stops duplicate charges.

examples.bad: I simply updated the config and it actually works now.
examples.better: I updated the config, and the import job now succeeds.

examples.bad: Honestly, the test suite is fundamentally broken.
examples.better: The test suite fails on a clean checkout: 12 tests depend on a local .env file.

examples.bad: The real problem is the honest shape of the data.
examples.better: Half the rows are missing a timestamp.

rules.source: stop-slop (hardikpandya/stop-slop); Humanizer (blader/humanizer); avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon)

rules.name: Use one name for one thing
rules.dont: Rotating synonyms for the same referent (the function, the helper, the utility, the method) to avoid repetition.
rules.do: Pick one name and keep it. Repetition is clearer than variety.
rules.rationale: Readers assume a new word means a new thing. Synonym cycling makes them wonder whether you mean one object or several.
detect: The same referent called by two or more different nouns within a reply

examples.bad: The parseDate function fails on ISO strings. The helper also ignores offsets, so the utility returns UTC.
examples.better: The parseDate function fails on ISO strings. parseDate also ignores offsets, so it returns UTC.

examples.bad: The protagonist meets a stranger. Later, the hero returns home, where the young man finds a letter.
examples.better: Anna meets a stranger. Later, Anna returns home and finds a letter.

examples.bad: Restart the worker. Once the daemon is up, check that the process is healthy.
examples.better: Restart the worker. After it starts, check that the worker is healthy.

examples.bad: Mad cow disease ... bovine spongiform encephalitis ...
examples.better: Pick one name and use it every time.
examples.note: Human-identified: CDC Simply Put: readers may think the two names are two diseases.

rules.source: Humanizer (blader/humanizer); zonderlabs.com/slop + x.com/zhizdev thread; Google developer documentation style guide; Federal Plain Language Guidelines (plainlanguage.gov / digital.gov); Microsoft Writing Style Guide; Mailchimp Content Style Guide; CDC Simply Put

rules.name: Don't use promotional language
rules.dont: Sales-brochure adjectives and puffery: nestled, breathtaking, stunning, rich history, world-class, best-in-class, cutting-edge, state-of-the-art, revolutionary, groundbreaking, comprehensive, mission-critical, empower.
rules.do: Describe the thing plainly, and give the specific fact that would earn the adjective.
rules.rationale: Puffery replaces specific facts with generic praise. The subject gets louder and blurrier at the same time. In Nielsen and Morkes's 1997 study, an objective rewrite of promotional web text scored 27% better on overall usability (only the satisfaction gain was statistically significant). A Sun customer in the same research put it plainly: they wanted fact, not platitudes.
detect: Any listed adjective used to praise rather than describe
'innovative' and other evaluation words are counted by WORD-13
rules.exceptions: Fine inside a quotation or when the term is literal ("state-of-the-art" in an ML benchmark table with the score).

examples.bad: Nestled in the breathtaking hills, the town boasts a rich history.
examples.better: The town, founded in 1854, is in the hills 20 miles north of Austin.

examples.bad: We built a comprehensive, cutting-edge test harness.
examples.better: The test harness covers all 34 API endpoints and runs in four minutes.

examples.bad: An innovative, best-in-class approach to caching.
examples.better: A caching layer that cut database reads by 70%.

rules.source: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; Humanizer (blader/humanizer); Declaude (danielrosehill/Declaude); Nielsen & Morkes, NN/g (1997)

rules.name: Keep the small words; write full sentences
rules.dont: Headline fragments, label-colon shorthand, and dropped articles: "Next: tune knobs", "Same algorithm, same numbers", "Done: tests green, PR up."
rules.do: Keep articles, verbs, and connecting words.
rules.rationale: Dropped words save the writer a few characters and cost the reader the relationships between ideas.
detect: Lines like 'Goal:', 'Next:', 'Net:', 'Status:' followed by fragments
Comma-joined noun phrases with no verb
Microsoft and Mailchimp: keep 'that', 'who', 'the', 'then', 'to'; they show sentence structure to readers and translation tools
Microsoft: put verbs in short headings and labels when needed ('Access is denied', not 'Access denied')
STE: don't omit verbs, subjects, or articles to shorten text
rules.exceptions: Labels are fine in real structured output (a commit template, a table).

examples.bad: Same algorithm, same numbers within ±2%.
examples.better: The CUDA version uses the same algorithm as the Triton one, and its timings are within 2%.

examples.bad: Recap: goal is faster kernel on H200; verified clone reproduces within 2% locally. Next: tune knobs, lab-check.
examples.better: We're trying to make the kernel faster on the H200. I confirmed the CUDA version matches Triton within 2% on this machine. Next I'll tune its settings and test it on the H200.

examples.bad: Done: tests green, lint clean, PR up.
examples.better: All tests and lint checks pass. I opened PR #214.

examples.bad: Empty container.
examples.better: Empty the container.
examples.note: Human-identified: Microsoft Writing Style Guide, global writing tips: without 'the', it can read as a noun phrase.

examples.bad: Inspect the database to verify all tables migrated.
examples.better: Inspect the database to verify that the migration copied every table.
examples.note: Human-identified: Adapted from the Microsoft Writing Style Guide: keep 'that'.

rules.source: zonderlabs.com/slop + x.com/zhizdev thread; Microsoft Writing Style Guide; Google developer documentation style guide; Mailchimp Content Style Guide; ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English (via Wikipedia)

rules.name: Watch for clusters of AI-favored verbs and adjectives
rules.dont: Two or more of these in one paragraph (avoid-ai-writing Tier 2): harness, navigate, foster, elevate, unleash, streamline, bolster, spearhead, resonate with, revolutionize, underpin, nuanced, crucial, vital, multifaceted, ecosystem (metaphor), myriad, plethora, encompass, catalyze, reimagine, galvanize, augment, cultivate, illuminate, elucidate, juxtapose, transformative, cornerstone, paramount, poised to, burgeoning, nascent, quintessential, overarching, quietly, garner, align with, highlight (verb), enhance, tailored, newfound.
rules.do: Keep one if it's the right word. Replace the rest with plain verbs (use, handle, support, improve, lead, simplify) or with the specific fact.
rules.rationale: Any one of these is normal English. Several together are a strong statistical tell, and they usually stand in for specifics.
detect: Count listed words per paragraph; flag at 2 or more
'quietly' as an intensifier ('quietly became the standard') counts
rules.exceptions: Technical senses don't count: a software ecosystem you name, "navigate to Settings", image augmentation.

examples.bad: To harness this momentum, we must foster a culture that elevates quality and streamlines delivery.
examples.better: We should add a required review step and cut the release checklist from 14 items to 6.

examples.bad: The tool quietly became the cornerstone of a burgeoning ecosystem.
examples.better: About 400 open-source projects depend on the tool.

examples.bad: This nuanced, multifaceted approach aligns with our overarching goals.
examples.better: This approach meets the two goals we set in Q3: faster builds and fewer flaky tests.

rules.source: avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon); Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; Antislop (sam-paech)

rules.name: Back up evaluative adjectives
rules.dont: Heavy use of unsupported evaluation words (avoid-ai-writing Tier 3): significant(ly), innovative/innovation, effective(ly), dynamic(s), scalable/scalability, compelling, unprecedented, exceptional(ly), remarkable/remarkably, sophisticated, instrumental, plus stock phrases like "the intersection of", "the integration of", "community-driven", "long-term sustainability", "user engagement", "emerging space".
rules.do: Replace the adjective with the number, comparison, or mechanism that earns it. Keep the word only where the evidence sits next to it.
rules.rationale: These are ordinary words, so one use means nothing. At high density they signal claims without evidence.
detect: Three or more hits in a short piece (or roughly 3% of words in a long one)
An evaluation word with no number or comparison in the same sentence
rules.exceptions: "Statistically significant" with a p-value is fine.

examples.bad: This innovative, scalable platform delivers significant and compelling results at the intersection of AI and finance.
examples.better: The platform processes 40,000 loan applications a day and approves them 3x faster than our old system.

examples.bad: The team played an instrumental role in this remarkable, unprecedented growth.
examples.better: The team built the referral program, which brought in 38% of new users last year.

rules.source: avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon)

rules.name: Replace slogans with behavior
rules.dont: Dev-blog and launch-copy slogans: zero config, it just works, batteries included, blazing fast, lightning fast, developer-friendly, out of the box, effortless, frictionless, plug and play, next-generation, enterprise-grade, production-ready (unqualified).
rules.do: Name the concrete behavior: what the user does, how long it takes, what the number is.
rules.rationale: Slogans are claims the reader can't check. The specific behavior is shorter to verify and more convincing.
detect: Any listed slogan without a measurement or concrete step next to it
rules.exceptions: Fine when followed immediately by the proof ("zero config: it reads your existing tsconfig").

examples.bad: A blazing-fast, zero-config bundler that just works.
examples.better: The bundler reads your existing tsconfig and builds a 50,000-line app in 1.2 seconds.

examples.bad: Enterprise-grade security out of the box.
examples.better: Every request is encrypted with TLS 1.3, and SSO with Okta takes one setting.

examples.bad: Effortless, frictionless onboarding.
examples.better: New users can import their data from a CSV in one step.

rules.source: avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon)

rules.name: State the point without a contrast setup
rules.dont: Negative parallelisms and reversals: "It's not X, it's Y", "not just X but also Y", "X isn't the problem. Y is.", "The question isn't X. It's Y.", "Y rather than X", and negative listing ("Not a X. Not a Y. A Z.").
rules.do: State Y directly. Mention X only if the reader actually believes X and needs correcting, and then name who believes it.
rules.rationale: The construction argues with a claim nobody made. It's one of the most recognized AI tells.
detect: not/isn't X, (but/it's) Y
not only/just X but (also) Y
Y rather than X as a closing contrast
Two or more 'Not a...' fragments before the real noun
Negation chains: 'No X. No Y. Just Z.' or 'It didn't X. It didn't Y.'
rules.exceptions: Fine when correcting a misconception the user actually stated, or when the contrast is the requested comparison.

examples.bad: This isn't a bug, it's a contract.
examples.better: The function is documented to return null on a miss, so this is expected.

examples.bad: The bottleneck isn't the database. It's the serializer.
examples.better: The serializer is the bottleneck. It takes 80% of request time.

examples.bad: Not a framework. Not a library. A way of thinking.
examples.better: It's a set of conventions for naming and testing services.

examples.bad: Rather than simply retelling the legend, the film reimagines it for modern audiences.
examples.better: The film moves the legend to present-day Shanghai.

examples.bad: No setup. No config. No headaches. Just results.
examples.better: It runs with the defaults in your package.json.

rules.source: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; Humanizer (blader/humanizer); stop-slop (hardikpandya/stop-slop); no-ai-slop (realrossmanngroup); zonderlabs.com/slop + x.com/zhizdev thread; avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon); Antislop (sam-paech))

rules.name: Don't force lists of three
rules.dont: Triplets added for rhythm: "fast, reliable, and scalable", "clear, concise, and actionable", three bullet points where two or four are real.
rules.do: Use the number of items you actually have. One strong item beats three padded ones.
rules.rationale: Three sounds complete, so LLMs pad to three. The third item is usually the weakest or a synonym of the first two.
detect: Three adjectives or short phrases in a row with no evidence behind each
Every list in a reply has exactly three items
A colon introducing exactly three items
Flags only when three or more triplets appear in one text; a single list of three is normal
rules.exceptions: Fine when there really are three things (three failing tests, three files).

examples.bad: The new API is fast, reliable, and scalable.
examples.better: The new API answers in under 50 ms at our peak load.

examples.bad: This approach is simpler, cleaner, and more maintainable.
examples.better: This approach removes the custom retry wrapper, which was 200 lines.

examples.bad: It preserves Nezha's image, weapons, and spirit while reshaping them through contemporary values, modern aesthetics, and digital animation.
examples.better: It keeps the original characters and moves the story to a modern setting.

rules.source: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; Humanizer (blader/humanizer); stop-slop (hardikpandya/stop-slop); no-ai-slop (realrossmanngroup); avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon)

rules.name: No aphorisms or punchlines
rules.dont: Epigrams and manufactured profundity: numbered maxims, "The gap is real but modest.", "That's it. That's the whole trick.", "Let that sink in.", one-line paragraphs built for punch, every paragraph ending on a zinger.
rules.do: State the claim plainly in a complete sentence and move on.
rules.rationale: Aphorisms compress the claim until the reader has to decode it. The source mocks these as "Claude Tzu".
detect: Short balanced or verbless lines that read like a proverb
'That's it.' / 'Full stop.' / 'Period.' / 'Let that sink in.'
One-sentence paragraphs used for drama
patterns: (?:^|[.!?]\s+)(?:That'?s it|Full stop|Period|Let that sink in|Make no mistake)\b[.!]?

examples.bad: The same ruler on both sides, and the gap is real but modest.
examples.better: We used the same benchmark for AI and human writing. AI scored somewhat worse.

examples.bad: Delete the cache. That's it. That's the whole fix.
examples.better: Deleting the stale cache fixes it.

examples.bad: Ship small. Ship often. Full stop.
examples.better: Smaller releases have caused fewer rollbacks for this team.

rules.source: zonderlabs.com/slop + x.com/zhizdev thread; stop-slop (hardikpandya/stop-slop); no-ai-slop (realrossmanngroup))

rules.name: Make the point instead of setting it up
rules.dont: Rhetorical setups: "What if...?" reframes, questions answered in the next sentence, "Think about it:", "Here's what I mean:", colon-then-reveal ("The fix is simple:"), pseudo-clefts ("What makes this hard is...").
rules.do: Say the point first, in the subject-verb order of a normal sentence.
rules.rationale: Setups delay the point and announce insight instead of delivering it.
detect: A question followed immediately by its own answer
'What [makes/matters/is X] is ...' sentence openers
'is simple/clear/easy:' followed by the reveal
Two or more rhetorical questions in a row
Mailchimp/CDC: questions as subheads are fine if they match questions readers actually ask
patterns: (?:^|[.!?]\s+)(?:Think about it|Here'?s what I mean|What if)\b
rules.exceptions: Real questions to the user are fine. So is a question heading in an FAQ.

examples.bad: Why does this matter? Because the cache never expires.
examples.better: The cache has no expiry, so users see stale prices.

examples.bad: What makes this hard is the lack of tests.
examples.better: There are no tests for the payment module, so every change is risky.

examples.bad: The fix is simple: delete one line.
examples.better: Deleting line 42 fixes it.

examples.bad: What if we stopped thinking of errors as failures?
examples.better: Treat expected errors as return values instead of exceptions.

examples.bad: Why does this happen? What can we do about it? The answer is simple.
examples.better: It happens because the cache key ignores the locale. Add the locale to the key.

rules.source: stop-slop (hardikpandya/stop-slop); no-ai-slop (realrossmanngroup); avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon); Federal Plain Language Guidelines (plainlanguage.gov / digital.gov)

rules.name: Drop trailing "-ing" commentary
rules.dont: A participle phrase tacked onto a fact to add significance: "..., highlighting its importance", "..., ensuring reliability", "..., reflecting the team's commitment", "..., contributing to".
rules.do: End the sentence after the fact. If the effect matters, state it as its own sentence with evidence.
rules.rationale: The tacked-on phrase is unsupported analysis. It usually claims an effect nobody measured.
detect: Comma + highlighting/underscoring/emphasizing/ensuring/reflecting/symbolizing/showcasing/contributing to/fostering/cultivating/enhancing
rules.exceptions: Fine when the participle states a real, checked consequence ("..., causing the build to fail").

examples.bad: I added input validation, ensuring robust and secure handling of user data.
examples.better: I added input validation. Requests with missing fields now get a 400.

examples.bad: The town has a population of 4,000, reflecting its enduring appeal.
examples.better: The town has a population of 4,000.

examples.bad: We moved to TypeScript, showcasing our commitment to code quality.
examples.better: We moved to TypeScript. The compiler caught 31 type errors during the move.

rules.source: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; Humanizer (blader/humanizer)

rules.name: Don't inflate significance
rules.dont: Claims of importance without the specific thing: "marks a pivotal moment", "a testament to", "plays a vital role", "sets the stage for", "represents a shift", "evolving landscape", "This matters because", "The implications are significant", "The stakes are high".
rules.do: Name the specific consequence, or cut the sentence.
rules.rationale: Inflation replaces a fact with a generic claim that could apply to anything. Readers learn to skip it.
detect: Significance words without a concrete consequence in the same sentence
Vague declaratives: implications/stakes/consequences + significant/high/real
Vague endorsement (worth reading, a must-read) without saying why
rules.exceptions: Fine when a cited source makes the claim, attributed by name.

examples.bad: This migration marks a pivotal moment for the platform.
examples.better: Every service now uses the same auth library.

examples.bad: The 2019 census data serves as a testament to the town's enduring growth.
examples.better: The town grew from 3,100 people in 2009 to 4,000 in 2019.

examples.bad: The implications are significant.
examples.better: If the token leaks, anyone can read every customer's invoices.

examples.bad: This matters because users depend on it.
examples.better: About 2,000 users run this export every Monday.

rules.source: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; Humanizer (blader/humanizer); stop-slop (hardikpandya/stop-slop); avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon)

rules.name: No false ranges
rules.dont: "From X to Y" where X and Y aren't ends of a real scale: "from startups to enterprises", "from bug fixes to new features", "from the boardroom to the break room".
rules.do: List the actual items, or give the real range with numbers.
rules.rationale: A false range suggests coverage of everything in between, which usually isn't true.
detect: 'from [noun] to [noun]' where the nouns are categories, not points on a scale
rules.exceptions: Real ranges are fine ("from 2019 to 2024", "from 10 ms to 40 ms").

examples.bad: It's used by everyone from startups to Fortune 500 companies.
examples.better: About 300 companies use it, including Stripe and two of the five largest US banks.

examples.bad: The PR covers everything from bug fixes to new features.
examples.better: The PR fixes two bugs and adds CSV export.

examples.bad: This guide takes you from beginner to expert.
examples.better: This guide covers setup, the core API, and deployment.

rules.source: Humanizer (blader/humanizer)

rules.name: End with a specific fact or next step
rules.dont: Formulaic endings: "Despite these challenges, X continues to thrive", "The future looks bright", "Exciting times ahead", "In conclusion", outline sections like "Challenges and Future Outlook".
rules.do: End on the last useful fact, the open question, or the concrete next step. Stop when you're done.
rules.rationale: Generic conclusions restate nothing specific and signal that the writer ran out of content.
detect: 'Despite (its/these) ... challenges'
'the future looks bright', 'exciting times', 'remains to be seen'
'In conclusion', 'Overall,' as the opener of a summary paragraph

examples.bad: Despite these challenges, the project continues to thrive.
examples.better: Two maintainers left in March. Releases slowed to one per quarter.

examples.bad: In conclusion, the migration was a success and the future looks bright.
examples.better: The migration finished with no downtime. Next, we'll remove the old tables on June 1.

examples.bad: Only time will tell whether the fix holds.
examples.better: I'll check the error rate tomorrow morning. If it's above 0.1%, I'll roll back.

rules.source: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; Humanizer (blader/humanizer)

rules.name: No hooks or launch-copy openers
rules.dont: Attention hooks and ad copy: "Imagine a world where...", "Picture this:", "The catch?", "Plot twist:", "Spoiler:", "Here's the kicker", "Meet X, your new favorite...", "But what does this mean for developers?", "N things you need to know", "This one is worth your time".
rules.do: Open with the fact or the news. End with the last useful fact.
rules.rationale: Hooks promise a payoff the text then has to deliver, and in technical writing the reader already chose to read.
detect: Sentence-initial hook phrase
Rhetorical question that introduces the next section

examples.bad: Imagine a world where deploys never fail. Meet Shipit, your new favorite CLI.
examples.better: Shipit is a CLI that rolls back a deploy automatically when health checks fail.

examples.bad: The catch? It only works on Linux.
examples.better: It only works on Linux.

examples.bad: But what does this mean for developers? Plot twist: you don't need to change anything.
examples.better: Existing code keeps working without changes.

rules.source: avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon); stop-slop (hardikpandya/stop-slop); no-ai-slop (realrossmanngroup)

rules.name: No false concessions or invented crowds
rules.dont: Concessions that stage balance without content ("While X is impressive, Y remains a challenge"), and contrasts against an imagined lagging group ("while everyone else was still debating", "unlike most tools", "most people don't realize").
rules.do: State the specific limitation, or name the real competitor and the real difference.
rules.rationale: The concession and the crowd are both invented to make the claim feel earned.
detect: 'While X is/was [praise], Y remains/is still [problem]'
Contrast with 'everyone else', 'most people', 'most tools' with no source
rules.exceptions: Real comparisons with named alternatives are fine.

examples.bad: While the results are impressive, scalability remains a challenge.
examples.better: The service handles 1,000 requests per second. Above that, the queue backs up.

examples.bad: While everyone else was still debating, we shipped.
