examples.better: We shipped in March, two months before the next comparable tool.

examples.bad: Unlike most tools, it respects your privacy.
examples.better: It stores nothing on our servers. Unlike Grammarly, it runs entirely offline.

rules.source: avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon)

rules.name: Delete throat-clearing and announcements
rules.dont: Openers and labels that announce content instead of giving it: "Here's the thing:", "Here's what I found", "The short version:", "Let me be clear", "It turns out", "Let me walk you through", "In this section, we'll", "Let's dive in", "Done:".
rules.do: Start with the content itself.
rules.rationale: Announcements cost reading time and push the point further down. Pinker calls this metadiscourse: signposting the text instead of writing it.
detect: A sentence or fragment that could be deleted with no loss
'Here's what/why/the' constructions
patterns: (?:^|\n|[.!?]\s+)(?:Here'?s\s+(?:the\s+(?:thing|key|catch|deal|kicker)|what|why|how)|What this (?:settles|means)|The short version|Bottom line|Key (?:insight|takeaway)|TL;DR|Short answer|Let me (?:be clear|explain|walk you through)|It turns out|The truth is|The reality is|Let'?s dive in|In this section)\b
\b(?:it'?s worth noting(?: that)?|it'?s important to note(?: that)?|needless to say|as we'?ll see)\b
rules.exceptions: "Here's the diff" is fine when it introduces an attached artifact.

examples.bad: Here's the key insight: the cache is never invalidated.
examples.better: No code path invalidates the cache.

examples.bad: It's worth noting that the API also supports pagination.
examples.better: The API also supports pagination.

examples.bad: Let me walk you through what I found. It turns out the token expired.
examples.better: The token expired.

examples.bad: Let's dive in! There are three ways to configure this.
examples.better: You can configure this in the CLI, in config.toml, or with environment variables.

rules.source: zonderlabs.com/slop + x.com/zhizdev thread; stop-slop (hardikpandya/stop-slop); no-ai-slop (realrossmanngroup); Humanizer (blader/humanizer); Pinker, The Sense of Style (2014)

rules.name: No chatbot openers or sign-offs
rules.dont: Service-desk phrases: "Certainly!", "Of course!", "Absolutely!", "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if you have any questions", "Would you like me to...?", "Is there anything else?", "Happy coding!".
rules.do: Start with the answer. End when the content ends. Offer a next step only when it is specific and likely wanted.
rules.rationale: These phrases are the clearest marker of chatbot text and carry no content.
detect: Exclamatory one-word openers
Closing offers or wishes
rules.exceptions: A specific offer is fine when the next step is real and the user would likely want it ("Want me to open the PR?").

examples.bad: Certainly! Here's the updated function.
examples.better: The updated function is below.

examples.bad: I hope this helps! Let me know if you have any other questions.
examples.better: (Delete.)

examples.bad: Would you like me to explain anything else or make further changes?
examples.better: I didn't touch the tests for the old endpoint. They'll fail until we delete them.

rules.source: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; Humanizer (blader/humanizer); no-ai-slop (realrossmanngroup)

rules.name: No flattery or validation
rules.dont: Praise and mind-reading aimed at the user: "Great question!", "You're absolutely right!", "Excellent point", "I understand your concern", "I see where you're coming from".
rules.do: Answer the question. If the user was right, say what you changed because of it.
rules.rationale: Flattery is filler, and agreeing too fast makes corrections less trustworthy.
detect: Praise of the question or the user
Claims about the user's feelings

examples.bad: Great question! The difference is that let is block-scoped.
examples.better: let is block-scoped. var is function-scoped.

examples.bad: You're absolutely right, I made a mistake there.
examples.better: The off-by-one was mine. I changed < to <= on line 18.

examples.bad: I understand your concern about performance.
examples.better: The new query adds about 3 ms per request.

rules.source: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; Humanizer (blader/humanizer)

rules.name: Hedge once, specifically
rules.dont: Stacked qualifiers and reflexive caution: "could potentially possibly", "it may be worth considering", "it seems like it might", "generally speaking, in most cases".
rules.do: Use one qualifier where real uncertainty exists, and say what it depends on. Otherwise state the claim.
rules.rationale: Stacked hedges hide how sure you are. One precise hedge tells the reader what to check. Pinker calls reflexive qualifiers ('somewhat', 'relatively', 'apparently') soggy apologies; keep a hedge only where you'd defend it.
detect: Two or more hedge words in one clause
'may be worth', 'might want to consider'
rules.exceptions: Medical, legal, and financial content may need explicit caveats. Keep them specific. The opposite failure is also real: CDC CCI item 11 asks that real uncertainty be stated (see CLR-18).

examples.bad: This could potentially possibly cause issues in some edge cases.
examples.better: This fails when the input list is empty.

examples.bad: It may be worth considering adding an index.
examples.better: Add an index on orders.user_id. The query scans 2M rows without it.

examples.bad: It seems like it might be a race condition.
examples.better: It's probably a race condition: it fails only with 4+ workers. I haven't confirmed it yet.

rules.source: Humanizer (blader/humanizer); Pinker, The Sense of Style (2014); CDC Clear Communication Index

rules.name: Name your sources
rules.dont: Vague authority and name-dropping: "experts say", "studies show", "industry reports", "observers have noted", "some critics argue", "widely regarded", "has been featured in major outlets".
rules.do: Name the source and what it said, or state the claim as your own with your evidence.
rules.rationale: Weasel attributions can't be checked, and LLMs often invent or inflate them.
detect: Unnamed plural authorities
Lists of outlet types instead of a specific citation

examples.bad: Experts agree that microservices improve scalability.
examples.better: Both of our outages last quarter came from timeouts between services. For a team of three, I'd keep the monolith.

examples.bad: Studies show that code review reduces bugs.
examples.better: Bacchelli and Bird (Microsoft Research, 2013) found that most review comments were about code quality, not defects.

examples.bad: The library has been featured in major tech outlets.
examples.better: The library has 18,000 GitHub stars, and 1,200 npm packages depend on it.

rules.source: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; Humanizer (blader/humanizer)

rules.name: Don't write gap-filling disclaimers
rules.dont: Disclaimers that point at missing information or tell the reader how to treat it: "While specific details are limited", "not widely documented", "based on available information", "as of my last update", "should be treated as X rather than Y", "does not by itself establish".
rules.do: Say what you checked and what you didn't find. If nothing useful remains, leave the topic out.
rules.rationale: These disclaimers are often speculative themselves and fill space where facts should be.
detect: Limited/scarce/not publicly available framing
'should be treated/viewed/understood as' corrective framing
Speculative fill: 'likely began', 'is believed to have', 'maintains a low profile'
rules.exceptions: Fine to say plainly that you couldn't verify something the user asked about. Distinguish from CLR-18: say what is known and unknown with a source, but don't add generic disclaimers.

examples.bad: While specific details are limited, the company likely focuses on enterprise clients.
examples.better: I couldn't find the company's customer list. Its site and LinkedIn page don't name any clients.

examples.bad: Based on available information, the function appears to be deprecated.
examples.better: The changelog for v3.2 marks this function as deprecated.

examples.bad: This benchmark should be treated as indicative rather than definitive.
examples.better: This benchmark ran on one machine with one dataset. Results on your hardware may differ.

rules.source: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; Humanizer (blader/humanizer); avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon)

rules.name: Cut wordy filler phrases
rules.dont: Padding: in order to, due to the fact that, at this point in time, in the event that, for the purpose of, when it comes to, at its core, in today's [X], in a world where, the fact that, a number of. Also Zinsser's clutter: 'personal friend', 'at the present time', 'I might add', 'it is interesting to note'; and Microsoft's openers 'you can' and 'there is/are' when they only delay the verb.
rules.do: Use the short form: to, because, now, if, for, about, many.
rules.rationale: Each phrase adds words and no meaning.
detect: Any listed phrase

examples.bad: In order to run the tests, you'll need Docker.
examples.better: To run the tests, you need Docker.

examples.bad: Due to the fact that the API is rate-limited, requests fail at this point in time.
examples.better: Requests fail now because the API is rate-limited.

examples.bad: When it comes to caching, at its core the issue is invalidation.
examples.better: Cache invalidation is the hard part.

examples.bad: We are currently in the process of consolidating our product range.
examples.better: We're selling fewer products.
examples.note: Human-identified: Plain English Campaign Golden Bull, 2003 (jungle.com). Rewrite is ours.

examples.bad: The following summary is intended only to highlight certain information contained elsewhere in this Prospectus.
examples.better: This summary highlights some information from this Prospectus.

examples.bad: You can access Office apps across your devices, and you get online file storage and sharing.
examples.better: Store files online, access them from all your devices, and share them with coworkers.
examples.note: Human-identified: Microsoft Writing Style Guide, top 10 tips.

examples.bad: There are many users who skip the setup step.
examples.better: Many users skip the setup step.

rules.source: Humanizer (blader/humanizer); stop-slop (hardikpandya/stop-slop); Plain English Campaign; 18F content guide; SEC Plain English Handbook (1998); Zinsser, On Writing Well (via LitCharts); Microsoft Writing Style Guide; Garner, LawProse Lesson 287

rules.name: No sweeping absolutes
rules.dont: Lazy extremes: always, never, every, everyone, nobody, all, completely, entirely, used as emphasis rather than measured fact.
rules.do: Give the actual scope or number.
rules.rationale: Absolutes are usually false, and readers stop trusting the claim when they find one exception.
detect: always/never/every/everyone/nobody in a claim with no count behind it
rules.exceptions: Fine when literally true and checked ("the job never ran: the cron entry is commented out").

examples.bad: Everyone uses this pattern.
examples.better: Most of the repos in this org use this pattern: 41 of 50.

examples.bad: This never works on Windows.
examples.better: This fails on Windows because the path uses forward slashes.

examples.bad: Nobody reads the docs.
examples.better: Docs page views dropped 60% after we added in-app help.

rules.source: stop-slop (hardikpandya/stop-slop)

rules.name: Don't tell the reader how to feel about a fact
rules.dont: Steering cues and performed insight: Notably, Interestingly, Surprisingly, Importantly, Crucially, "Here's what's interesting", "the key point", "the contrarian take", "sit with that for a moment", "worth naming", "I want to be upfront", "To be honest", "Honestly?", "What surprised me most", "I can't stop thinking about".
rules.do: State the fact and let it carry its own weight. If something is surprising, show what was expected and what happened.
rules.rationale: Steering cues pre-interpret the content. When the fact is strong they're redundant, and when it's weak they're false.
detect: Sentence-initial calibration adverb + comma
Labels that grade the writer's own point (key, contrarian, important)
Announcing candor instead of being candid

examples.bad: Interestingly, the bug only appears on Tuesdays.
examples.better: The bug appears only on Tuesdays, when the weekly report job runs.

examples.bad: I want to be upfront: I haven't tested this on Windows.
examples.better: I haven't tested this on Windows.

examples.bad: Here's what's surprising: the old version was faster.
examples.better: I expected the rewrite to be faster, but the old version runs in 80 ms and the new one in 120 ms.

rules.source: avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon); stop-slop (hardikpandya/stop-slop)

rules.name: Don't restate the request
rules.dont: Openers that echo the user's question or praise their work before answering: "You're asking about X.", "So you want to...", "Great work on the PR! You've added X and Y...", "Let me make sure I understand..." when nothing is ambiguous.
rules.do: Start with the answer. Restate the request only when it's ambiguous, and then say which reading you chose.
rules.rationale: Echoing the prompt adds a paragraph of nothing and delays the answer.
detect: First sentence paraphrases the user's message
Opening praise that summarizes the user's own work back to them
rules.exceptions: Restating is fine when the request is ambiguous; name the interpretation in one clause.

examples.bad: You're asking how to make the build faster. Build speed is an important topic. The main option is caching.
examples.better: Turn on Turborepo's remote cache. It skips unchanged packages.

examples.bad: So you want to rename the column without downtime. Great question! Here's how.
examples.better: Add the new column, write to both, backfill, switch reads, then drop the old column.

examples.bad: Great work on this PR! You've added retries, refactored the client, and updated the docs.
examples.better: Two issues before merge: the retry loop has no cap, and the docs still show the old flag name.

rules.source: avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon)

rules.name: Drop scaffolding transitions
rules.dont: Essay connectors that add no logic: Moreover, Furthermore, Additionally, In addition, Thus, Hence, That said, On the other hand (with no first hand), As previously mentioned, As noted above, In terms of, and "Let's" + verb as a transition ("Let's look at", "Let's explore").
rules.do: Let sentence order carry the connection. Use "also", "so", or "but" when you need a connector.
rules.rationale: Formal connectors make prose sound like a school essay, and antislop measured several of them as heavily over-used by LLMs.
detect: Sentence-initial formal connector
'Let's' + verb that introduces the next section
rules.exceptions: "Thus" is fine in math proofs.

examples.bad: Moreover, the API is rate-limited. Furthermore, it lacks pagination.
examples.better: The API is also rate-limited, and it has no pagination.

examples.bad: Let's take a closer look at the error.
examples.better: The error comes from line 88, where config is undefined.

examples.bad: In terms of performance, the new query is better.
examples.better: The new query is 4x faster.

rules.source: avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon); Antislop (sam-paech)

rules.name: Lead with the point
rules.dont: Long front-loaded clauses, background, or process narration before the answer: "After looking through the codebase and weighing options, the cleanest path seems to be...".
rules.do: Put the answer, result, or decision in the first sentence. Reasons come after.
rules.rationale: The reader decides from the first sentence whether to keep reading. A buried point takes several readings to find. The U.S. Army's BLUF standard puts the main point first. In Kimble's survey of 251 Michigan lawyers, an opening summary was a top reason 61% preferred the plain-language judicial opinion. HHS found that many readers with limited literacy read only the first few words of a page or paragraph before deciding whether to continue.
detect: First sentence opens with a long subordinate clause (After, Since, Given, Having, Based on)
The requested result appears after the first comma-heavy clause
CDC Clear Communication Index items 1-2: one main message (1-3 short sentences) in the first paragraph or section, visible without scrolling on the web
Simply Put: restate the main message at the end with the action

examples.bad: Nothing else depends on anything but the result, so I'll report as soon as the poll returns.
examples.better: I'll report the result when the poll finishes.

examples.bad: After looking through the codebase and weighing a few options, the cleanest path seems to be adding a flag to the existing handler.
examples.better: Add a flag to the existing handler. It's the smallest change, and nothing else calls that handler.

examples.bad: Given that the tests were flaky before and the CI runner has been slow this week, it's likely the failure isn't from your change.
examples.better: Your change probably didn't cause this failure. The test was flaky before your PR.

examples.bad: Blood pressure is the force of blood pushing against the walls of your arteries. It's important to get it checked often.
examples.better: Check your blood pressure every 2 years, especially if you are age 40 or older.
examples.note: Human-identified: HHS Health Literacy Online, section 2.3.

rules.source: zonderlabs.com/slop + x.com/zhizdev thread; Army Regulation 25-50 (BLUF); Nielsen & Morkes, NN/g (1997); Kimble, Writing for Dollars, Writing to Please (2012); CDC Clear Communication Index; HHS Health Literacy Online (2016); CDC Simply Put

rules.name: One main point per sentence
rules.dont: Sentences that carry several claims joined by semicolons, parentheses, and "since" clauses. Also any sentence over about 25 words (GOV.UK's split point), and an average above about 20.
rules.do: Split them. Aim for under about 25 words, one claim each.
rules.rationale: Packing a number, a cause, a constraint, and a plan into one sentence makes the reader hold all of them at once.
detect: More than ~30 words
A semicolon and a parenthetical in the same sentence
Three or more numbers in one sentence
Sentences over ~25 words (GOV.UK); averages above ~20. In Kimble's and Flammer's studies, plain versions that readers preferred averaged 18 to 19 words.
Federal guidelines: express only one idea in each sentence

Sentence-length targets by source: Simply Put 8-10 words; Flesch about 15 (conversational) to 20 (plain); HHS and usability.gov 20 or fewer; STE 20 for instructions, 25 for descriptions; GOV.UK and Mailchimp 25 or fewer
Microsoft: don't join more than three clauses with and, or, or but; preferably two

Semicolons are fine used sparingly: at most one per sentence, joining two closely related independent clauses. Don't chain clauses with them (Mailchimp avoids them entirely; owner decision: allow sparingly).
Several commas plus end punctuation usually signal a sentence to split (Microsoft)
rules.exceptions: Long sentences are fine when they're a simple list.

examples.bad: The one remaining warm-regime gap (o: 12.3 vs 7.9 µs) is purely stage depth, since the 10-stage instantiation exceeds this GPU's 101,376-byte limit by 1 KB; 8 or 9 stages will close it.
examples.better: One kernel is still slower: o takes 12.3 µs vs. 7.9 µs. The cause is pipeline depth. Ten stages need 1 KB more shared memory than this GPU has, so I'll try 8 or 9.
examples.note: From the source's Claude Code sample.

examples.bad: I fixed the import (it was pointing at the old path); the test still fails but now on an assertion (expected 3, got 2), which suggests the off-by-one is real.
examples.better: I fixed the broken import. The test still fails, but now on an assertion: it expected 3 and got 2. So the off-by-one bug is real.

examples.bad: (An 81-word opening sentence on a deferred-action form.)
examples.better: Split it into one sentence per requirement, and put the required action first.
examples.note: Human-identified: Center for Plain Language WonderMark award (Department of Homeland Security form). Described, not quoted.

examples.bad: The proposal is presented to an employer who agrees to negotiate an individualized job that meets the employment needs of the applicant and real business needs of the employer.
examples.better: We prepare a preliminary proposal to present to an employer who agrees to negotiate a job that meets both his and your employment needs.
examples.note: Human-identified: Federal Plain Language Guidelines, 'Write short sentences.' The guideline also puts 'you' and 'we' in place of 'the applicant' and passives.

examples.bad: (A 630-word single sentence in a council footpath-diversion notice, describing the route in metres from building corners.)
examples.better: Describe the route in short steps, or show it on a map.
examples.note: Human-identified: Plain English Campaign Golden Bull, 2005 (Halton Borough Council). Described, not quoted.

rules.source: zonderlabs.com/slop + x.com/zhizdev thread; GOV.UK style guide; Federal Plain Language Guidelines (plainlanguage.gov / digital.gov); Microsoft Writing Style Guide; Kimble (2012); HHS Health Literacy Online (2016); CDC Simply Put; Research-Based Web Design & Usability Guidelines (usability.gov), ch. 15; Mailchimp Content Style Guide; ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English (via Wikipedia); Flesch, How to Write Plain English; Federal Plain Language Guidelines (2011), via plainlanguage.gov archive; Plain English Campaign examples

rules.name: Put emphasis where the importance is
rules.dont: Bad news in a trailing clause or labeled as an aside ("One negative finding:", "Minor note:"), and trivia in the headline.
rules.do: Lead with what the user must act on, including failures, crashes, and caveats.
rules.rationale: Once the emphasis is right, the rest becomes a style choice. When it's wrong, the reader misses the one thing that mattered.
detect: Negative results introduced as an aside
A crash, data loss, or failing test mentioned after routine details

examples.bad: One negative finding: cp.async with an L2 evict-first hint is harmful on sm_120 (turns warm into cold) and crashed once, so it is out.
examples.better: Don't use cp.async with the L2 evict-first hint on sm_120. It made repeated runs as slow as first runs, and it crashed once. I removed it.
examples.note: From the source's Claude Code sample.

examples.bad: Refactored the helpers and updated the docs. Minor note: two tests are now failing.
examples.better: Two tests now fail after my refactor. I'm fixing them. I also updated the docs.

rules.source: zonderlabs.com/slop + x.com/zhizdev thread

rules.name: Say what you checked
rules.dont: Bare completion claims: "Done.", "Verified.", "Works now.", "Should be fine.", "All good."
rules.do: Say what you did and what you observed, and what you didn't check.
rules.rationale: "Verified" without the check is an empty statement. The reader can't tell how much to trust it.
detect: done/verified/confirmed/works/settled with no description of the check
'should' claims about untested behavior presented as results

examples.bad: Done: the Triton code is read, and the CUDA clone reproduces it.
examples.better: I read the Triton kernel and ported it to CUDA. On this GPU, the CUDA version's timings are within 2% of Triton's.
examples.note: From the source's Claude Code sample.

examples.bad: Verified, everything works.
examples.better: I ran the test suite (all 118 pass) and loaded the settings page. The new toggle saves correctly.

examples.bad: Should be fine now.
examples.better: I restarted the worker, and the queue has drained. I haven't checked the overnight job yet.

rules.source: zonderlabs.com/slop + x.com/zhizdev thread

rules.name: Vary sentence rhythm
rules.dont: Metronomic prose: every sentence the same length, stacks of short punchy fragments, or every paragraph ending on a one-liner.
rules.do: Mix short and long sentences the way the content needs. Use complete sentences.
rules.rationale: Uniform rhythm is a strong tell (Wikipedia notes a mid-2026 trend toward a strict 8 to 20 word band), and staccato fragments read as manufactured drama.
detect: Five or more consecutive sentences within a few words of the same length
Three or more fragments under five words in a row
Three or more consecutive sentences starting with the same word
rules.exceptions: Fragments are fine in UI labels, commit subjects, and lists. Starting a sentence with And or But is fine (Flesch).

examples.bad: It's fast. It's simple. It works. Ship it.
examples.better: It's fast and simple, and it passed every test, so I'd ship it.

examples.bad: The build failed. I checked the logs. The cache was stale. I cleared it. The build passed.
examples.better: The build failed because the cache was stale. After I cleared it, the build passed.

examples.bad: It reads the file. It parses the rows. It writes the output.
examples.better: It reads the file, parses each row, and writes the output to out.csv.

rules.source: stop-slop (hardikpandya/stop-slop); no-ai-slop (realrossmanngroup); Humanizer (blader/humanizer); Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon); Flesch, How to Write Plain English

rules.name: Describe what is, not what changed
rules.dont: Docs and code comments that narrate the edit: "now uses", "replaces the previous approach", "we changed X to Y", "updated to support", "no longer", "(new)", "refactored to".
rules.do: Describe current behavior as if it had always been this way. Put history in the commit message or changelog.
rules.rationale: A reader of the docs next year has no idea what "now" or "previous" refers to. The diff belongs in version control.
detect: 'now' + verb in documentation or a code comment (not in chat status reports)
References to a previous or old approach outside a changelog
rules.exceptions: Changelogs, migration guides, release notes, commit messages, and chat replies reporting what you just did are about change and are exempt.

examples.bad: // Now uses a Map instead of the old array lookup for speed.
examples.better: // Map lookup keeps this O(1) on large inputs.

examples.bad: The config loader replaces the previous YAML approach and now reads TOML.
examples.better: The config loader reads TOML from ./config.toml.

examples.bad: This function was refactored to support pagination.
examples.better: This function returns results one page at a time. Pass a cursor to get the next page.

rules.source: avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon)

rules.name: Make every paragraph add something
rules.dont: Paragraphs that restate the premise (the treadmill), paragraphs that could swap places without loss, and jumps between paragraphs with no connecting idea.
rules.do: Give each paragraph one new fact, claim, or step, and order them so each depends on the one before.
rules.rationale: If paragraphs can be reshuffled freely, the piece is a list of points, not an argument.
detect: A paragraph whose main claim already appeared earlier
Two body paragraphs that read the same in either order
A topic change with no bridge sentence
rules.exceptions: Reference material and FAQs are meant to be read out of order.

examples.bad: Caching is important for performance. [...] As mentioned, caching improves speed. [...] In short, caching makes things faster.
examples.better: Caching cut p95 latency from 900 ms to 200 ms. The risk is stale data, so entries expire after 60 seconds.

examples.bad: Paragraph 1: Our API is fast. Paragraph 2: Our API is secure. Paragraph 3: Our API is easy.
examples.better: The API is fast because responses come from an edge cache, and caching only public data keeps it secure.

rules.source: avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon)

rules.name: Use em dashes exceedingly sparingly
rules.dont: More than one em dash in a reply or short document; em dashes for dramatic reveals, asides that should be their own sentence, or paired dashes around a clause; spaced hyphens or double hyphens standing in for dashes.
rules.do: Default to a comma, parentheses, a colon, or a period. Keep at most one em dash in a piece, and only where no other punctuation works as well (for example, an inline definition: 'vomiting—throwing up—').
rules.rationale: Em-dash density is one of the most recognized AI tells, and dash asides usually hide a second sentence. Style guides allow em dashes (Mailchimp, Microsoft, HHS), so the rule limits rather than bans them.
detect: Two or more em dashes in one reply or short document
Any em dash introducing a punchline or reveal
' - ' or '--' used as a dash
rules.exceptions: Quoted text and code are exempt. Use an en dash (–) for numeric ranges. One em dash for an inline definition or a sharp break is acceptable.

examples.bad: The fix is small — just one line — but it matters.
examples.better: The fix is one line.

examples.bad: We tried three approaches — caching, batching, and indexing — and only indexing helped.
examples.better: We tried caching, batching, and indexing. Only indexing helped.

examples.bad: The result was clear — the old version was faster.
examples.better: The old version was faster.

rules.source: stop-slop (hardikpandya/stop-slop); Humanizer (blader/humanizer); no-ai-slop (realrossmanngroup); Owner decision (style review, Nov 2026)

rules.name: Emphasize sparingly: no bold sprawl, no ALL CAPS prose
rules.dont: Bold on ordinary words, on every key term, or on several phrases per paragraph. Also prose in ALL CAPS, and combining bold, italics, caps, and underline.
rules.do: Use plain text. Bold at most one warning or decision the reader must not miss.
rules.rationale: When everything is bold, nothing stands out, and the page reads like an ad. usability.gov 15:6 and Simply Put: all caps slows reading of running text.
detect: More than one bold span per paragraph
Bold on a term that isn't a warning, a UI label, or a defined term
rules.exceptions: UI labels the user must click can be bold ("Click **Save**").

examples.bad: This is a **critical** step that **significantly** improves **performance**.
examples.better: This step cuts load time from 3 s to 1 s.

examples.bad: Make sure to **always** run **migrations** before **deploying**.
examples.better: Run migrations before you deploy. **The app crashes on start if you don't.**

examples.bad: DO NOT PAY THE CIVIL ENFORCEMENT OFFICER
examples.better: Do not pay the traffic warden.
examples.note: Human-identified: Plain English Campaign before-and-after (parking ticket).

rules.source: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; Humanizer (blader/humanizer); Research-Based Web Design & Usability Guidelines (usability.gov), ch. 15; CDC Simply Put; Mailchimp Content Style Guide

rules.name: Use prose instead of label-colon bullets
rules.dont: Bullet lists where each item starts with a bold label and a colon ("**Performance:** ..."), especially for content that is one connected argument.
rules.do: Write a paragraph. Use a plain list only for discrete, parallel items, and keep the items short.
rules.rationale: Inline-header lists fragment reasoning and look templated.
detect: Two or more consecutive bullets starting with **Label:**
Five or more parallel bullet fragments with no verbs
rules.exceptions: Reference material (a glossary, a config table, an API field list) can use labeled items.

examples.bad:
- **Speed:** It's faster.
- **Cost:** It's cheaper.
- **Ease:** It's simpler.
examples.better: The new runner is about twice as fast and costs half as much, and it needs no custom config.

examples.bad:
- **Root cause:** stale cache
- **Fix:** clear on deploy
- **Next steps:** add a test
examples.better: The cause was a stale cache. I now clear it on every deploy, and I'll add a test that catches this.

rules.source: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; Humanizer (blader/humanizer); Declaude (danielrosehill/Declaude); avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon)

rules.name: Write plain, sentence-case headings
rules.dont: Title Case Headings, dramatic or clever headings ("The Pricing Trap", "The Hidden Cost of Convenience"), emoji in headings, and wrong heading levels (several H1s).
rules.do: Use sentence case, and say what the section contains.
rules.rationale: A heading is a label for skimming. Clever headings make the reader read the section to learn what it's about.
detect: Three or more capitalized words in a heading
Heading that is 'The [Adjective] [Noun]' with no topic word
Emoji in a heading
rules.exceptions: Proper nouns keep their capitals.

examples.bad: ## The Hidden Cost Of Convenience
examples.better: ## Subscriptions add up

examples.bad: ## Key Benefits And Considerations
examples.better: ## Trade-offs

examples.bad: ## 🚀 Getting Started
examples.better: ## Setup

examples.bad: ## Seat Belts
examples.better: ## Wear your seat belt. It could save your life.
examples.note: Human-identified: CDC Simply Put: complete-idea headings instead of one-word labels.

examples.bad: ## Find a Microsoft Partner
examples.better: ## Find a Microsoft partner
examples.note: Human-identified: Microsoft Writing Style Guide: sentence case.

rules.source: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; Humanizer (blader/humanizer); no-ai-slop (realrossmanngroup); CDC Simply Put; Microsoft Writing Style Guide; Mailchimp Content Style Guide

rules.name: Match structure to length
rules.dont: Headers, bullets, and tables on short answers; headings followed by one line; tables that repeat what the prose said; more than three heading levels.
rules.do: Answer short questions in a paragraph. Give each heading at least a few sentences of prose. Use tables only for real comparisons and lists only for discrete items or steps.
rules.rationale: Over-structuring fragments the reasoning and makes a simple answer look like a report.
detect: Headings in a reply under ~200 words
A heading followed by fewer than two sentences
A table restating earlier prose
H4 or deeper in a short document
Formulaic headings: Overview, Introduction, Key Takeaways, Conclusion, in a short piece
Opposite failure: a chat reply of 4+ sentences on several topics with no paragraph break
GOV.UK: no more than five sentences per paragraph
CDC CCI item 8: split lists over seven items; Simply Put: 3-7 items
rules.exceptions: Long reference documents and step-by-step procedures can use more structure.

examples.bad:
## Answer

- Yes

## Details

- It's supported since v2.
examples.better: Yes. Version 2 added it.

examples.bad:
| Option | Description |
|---|---|
| A | The first option |
| B | The second option |
examples.better: You have two options: A keeps the old schema, and B migrates it.

rules.source: Declaude (danielrosehill/Declaude); Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon); GOV.UK style guide; Nielsen & Morkes, NN/g (1997); Research-Based Web Design & Usability Guidelines (usability.gov), ch. 15; CDC Simply Put; CDC Clear Communication Index

rules.name: No emoji
rules.dont: Emoji in prose, headings, bullets, commit messages, code comments, or docs.
rules.do: Use plain text.
rules.rationale: Emoji bullets and headings are a common chatbot tell and look unprofessional in technical writing.
detect: Any emoji character
rules.exceptions: Fine when the user asks for them or when quoting UI text that contains them.

examples.bad: 🚀 Deployed to production! ✅
examples.better: Deployed to production.

examples.bad:
- ✨ New: dark mode
- 🐛 Fixed: login bug
examples.better:
- Added dark mode.
- Fixed the login redirect bug.

examples.bad: // 🔥 hot path, be careful
examples.better: // Hot path: runs on every request.

rules.source: Declaude (danielrosehill/Declaude); Humanizer (blader/humanizer); Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; no-ai-slop (realrossmanngroup)

rules.name: Match the destination's markup
rules.dont: Markdown where it won't render (wikitext, plain-text email, Slack fields that don't parse it), curly quotes in code or config, smart apostrophes in shell commands, leaked citation markup.
rules.do: Use the target format's own syntax, and straight quotes in anything a machine will parse.
rules.rationale: Wrong markup shows up as stray asterisks and pound signs, and curly quotes break code.
detect: Markdown syntax in a non-Markdown destination
Curly quotes inside code spans, commands, or config
Leaked tool markup (contentReference, oaicite, utm_source=chatgpt.com)
rules.exceptions: Curly quotes are fine in typeset prose if the destination uses them consistently.

examples.bad: git commit -m “fix login”
examples.better: git commit -m "fix login"

examples.bad: **Note:** see the [docs](https://example.org) (in a plain-text email)
examples.better: Note: see the docs at https://example.org

examples.bad: The study found a 12% drop.:contentReference[oaicite:1]
examples.better: The study found a 12% drop (Smith 2024).

rules.source: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing; Humanizer (blader/humanizer); avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon)

rules.name: Leave no placeholders
rules.dont: Unfilled template text: [Name], [Year], (Add URL here), 2025-XX-XX, example.com/source1, INSERT_URL, TODO left in delivered prose.
rules.do: Fill in the real value, or say plainly what is missing and ask for it.
rules.rationale: Placeholders in delivered text show it was never read, and they get published by accident.
detect: Square-bracket placeholders
XX dates
example.com subpaths
INSERT_ or ADD_ tokens
rules.exceptions: Templates the user asked for are supposed to have placeholders.

examples.bad: Travomate was founded in [Year] by [Founder Names].
examples.better: I couldn't find Travomate's founding year or founders. Do you have them?

examples.bad: access-date=2025-XX-XX
examples.better: access-date=2025-11-11

examples.bad: Official website: (Add your URL here)
examples.better: (Delete the line, or ask for the URL.)

rules.source: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing

rules.name: Don't create files nobody asked for
rules.dont: Unrequested documentation files (ARCHITECTURE.md, ROADMAP.md, SUMMARY.md, NOTES.md), summary files after a task, and ALL-CAPS filenames other than README.md.
rules.do: Put brief instructions in an existing file or in the reply. Create a doc only when asked or when the project can't run without it.
rules.rationale: Extra docs go stale, clutter the repo, and repeat what the code or the reply already says.
detect: New .md files the user didn't request
Uppercase filenames besides README, LICENSE, CHANGELOG
rules.exceptions: Conventional files are fine: README.md, LICENSE, CHANGELOG.md, CONTRIBUTING.md.

examples.bad: I've created IMPLEMENTATION_SUMMARY.md documenting all the changes.
examples.better: I changed three files: auth.ts, session.ts, and the login test.

examples.bad: I also added ARCHITECTURE.md and ROADMAP.md for future reference.
examples.better: (Don't create them. Mention architecture notes in the reply if they matter.)

rules.source: Declaude (danielrosehill/Declaude)

rules.name: Hyphenate only compound modifiers
rules.dont: Hyphens on compounds that aren't modifying a noun or aren't compounds at all: "in real-time", "follow-up with" (verb), "set-up the server" (verb), "log-in to" (verb), "data-set", "e-mail", and long hyphen chains ("cross-functional, data-driven, cloud-native").
rules.do: Hyphenate before a noun ("a real-time feed"), not after a verb ("updates in real time"). Use the closed forms: dataset, email, follow up, set up, log in.
rules.rationale: Over-hyphenation is a measurable AI habit and a common style error.
detect: Adverbial 'in real-time'
Hyphenated verb forms followed by a preposition or object
Three or more hyphenated modifiers in one sentence
rules.exceptions: Nouns keep their hyphens or closed forms per your style guide (a follow-up, a sign-up form).

examples.bad: The dashboard updates in real-time.
examples.better: The dashboard updates in real time.

examples.bad: Can you follow-up with the vendor and set-up the server?
examples.better: Can you follow up with the vendor and set up the server?

examples.bad: A cross-functional, data-driven, cloud-native, AI-powered team.
examples.better: A team of four engineers and a data analyst.

rules.source: avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon)

rules.name: Keep hashtags to a minimum
rules.dont: Hashtag stuffing: five or more hashtags on a post, hashtags inside sentences, generic tags (#innovation #leadership #AI #growth).
rules.do: Use zero to two specific hashtags at the end, or none.
rules.rationale: Hashtag walls read as automated posting and get worse reach on most platforms.
detect: Five or more hashtags in one post
Hashtags on generic words
rules.exceptions: Event or campaign tags the user asked for are fine.

examples.bad: Excited to share our launch! #AI #innovation #leadership #growth #startup #future
examples.better: We launched today. Here's the demo: (link) #DevTools

examples.bad: We're #hiring a #senior #engineer!
examples.better: We're hiring a senior backend engineer.

rules.source: avoid-ai-writing (conorbronsdon)

rules.name: Use exclamation points rarely
rules.dont: More than one exclamation point at a time, several in one message, and any exclamation point in an error or warning.
rules.do: End with a period. Save one exclamation point for genuine excitement in casual copy.
rules.rationale: Mailchimp: never more than one at a time, and never in error messages or alerts. Repeated exclamation points read as forced enthusiasm, a chatbot habit.
detect: !! or more
Two or more exclamation points in a short message
An exclamation point in an error, failure, or warning

examples.bad: Oops! Something went wrong!
examples.better: Something went wrong. Your changes weren't saved. Try again in a minute.

examples.bad: Great job!! Your file uploaded!
examples.better: Your file uploaded.

rules.source: Mailchimp Content Style Guide

rules.name: Punctuate 'but' by the grammar
rules.dont: Leaving out the comma when 'but' joins two independent clauses, or adding one when 'but' joins two verbs that share a subject.
rules.do: Put a comma before 'but' when each side could stand alone as a sentence ('The fix works, but the test still fails'). Leave it out when the second part has no subject of its own ('The fix works but needs a test'). Very short, closely linked clauses may drop the comma.
rules.rationale: Standard American usage (Chicago, AP, and most grammar references) puts a comma before a coordinating conjunction that joins two independent clauses. The comma tells the reader a new clause is starting.
detect: 'but' followed by a subject and verb with no comma before it
', but' followed directly by a verb with no subject (compound predicate)
rules.exceptions: The comma can go when both clauses are very short and closely connected ('It's slow but it works'). A comma before a contrasting phrase without a verb ('still fails, but now on an assertion') is acceptable.

examples.bad: The fix handles logged-in users but guest checkout still fails.
examples.better: The fix handles logged-in users, but guest checkout still fails.

examples.bad: The script runs locally, but fails in CI.
examples.better: The script runs locally but fails in CI.
examples.note: One subject, two verbs: no comma.

examples.bad: I updated the config but the tests still fail.
examples.better: I updated the config, but the tests still fail.

rules.source: Owner decision (style review, Nov 2026); Chicago Manual of Style and AP Stylebook (comma before a conjunction joining independent clauses)

rules.name: Always use the serial (Oxford) comma
rules.dont: Lists of three or more items with no comma before the final 'and' or 'or': 'Linux, macOS and Windows'.
rules.do: Put a comma before the conjunction in every list of three or more: 'Linux, macOS, and Windows'.
rules.rationale: The serial comma prevents misreading when list items contain 'and' or could be read as an appositive, and it keeps lists consistent. Chicago, Microsoft, Google, and Mailchimp all require it; AP is the main guide that doesn't.
detect: Three or more list items with no comma before the final 'and' or 'or'
Lists inside headings, bullets, and UI strings count too
rules.exceptions: Quoted text keeps its original punctuation. Items that themselves contain 'and' ('rise and grind') can trip the pattern; check by eye.

examples.bad: We support Linux, macOS and Windows.
examples.better: We support Linux, macOS, and Windows.

rules.name: Avoid stock fiction phrasing
rules.dont: The phrases LLM fiction repeats most, per Antislop's measured lists: took a deep breath, voice barely above a whisper, couldn't help but feel, couldn't shake the feeling, a shiver down (her) spine, casting long shadows, heart pounding in (his) chest, the air was thick with, words hung in the air, a mixture of, something akin to, a newfound sense of purpose, eyes never leaving, ready to face whatever challenges lay ahead, little did (he) know, days turned into weeks.
rules.do: Write the specific physical action or detail this character in this scene would have. If a beat adds nothing, cut it.
rules.rationale: These phrases are statistically over-represented in model-written stories by large factors. Readers of AI fiction recognize them on sight.
detect: Any listed phrase
More than one breath/whisper/shiver beat per scene
rules.exceptions: Fine in deliberate pastiche or when the cliché is the joke.

examples.bad: She took a deep breath, her voice barely above a whisper. "We need to go."
examples.better: "We need to go," she said, already pulling on her boots.

examples.bad: He couldn't shake the feeling that something was wrong. A shiver ran down his spine.
examples.better: The porch light was off. He'd left it on.

examples.bad: Days turned into weeks, and she found a newfound sense of purpose.
examples.better: By March she was at the workshop every morning before seven.

rules.name: Don't use default AI character and place names
rules.dont: Names LLMs reach for constantly: Elara, Kael, Lyra, Elias, Silas, Thorne, Aria, Elian, Mara, Lila, Seraphina, Zephyr; places like Eldoria, Oakhaven, Whisperwood, Ravenswood, Moonwhisper.
rules.do: Choose names that fit the setting's culture, era, and class, the way a writer researching the setting would.
rules.rationale: These names top Antislop's frequency lists by wide margins. One of them in the first line marks a story as generated.
detect: Any listed name for an original character or place
rules.exceptions: Fine when the user supplies the name or the character is an existing one.

examples.bad: Elara Thorne stood at the edge of Whisperwood.
examples.better: Dot Kowalski stood at the edge of the county landfill.

examples.bad: Kael and Lyra rode toward Eldoria.
examples.better: Ahmet and his sister rode toward Konya.
